entities/erasmus-in-venice.title: Erasmus in Venice
entities/erasmus-in-venice.content:
Erasmus in Venice
Desiderius Erasmus Roterodamus (1466–1536) was the most influential humanist of the Northern Renaissance — a Dutch scholar, theologian, satirist, and editor whose association with the Aldine Press in Venice produced one of the most successful books of the age. His Venetian sojourn, though brief (c. 1507–1508), marked a decisive turning point in his career and cemented the international reputation of Aldus Manutius’ workshop.
Arrival in Venice (1507–1508)
Erasmus arrived in Venice in late 1507, after a period of study in Paris and England, drawn by the Aldine Press’s growing fame as a centre of Greek and Latin scholarship. The issue of whether printing helped or hindered scholarship was still very much alive when “Erasmus visited Venice in 1507” (Lowry, p. 86). He came specifically to prepare a greatly expanded edition of his Adagia with Aldus, having first approached the printer by letter on 28 October 1507. In that letter, Erasmus had to “sell” his work to Aldus — offering his translations of Euripides’ Hecuba and Iphigeneia in Aulis, stressing favourable opinions from mutual friends, and even offering to bear the cost of up to 200 copies (Lowry, pp. 158–159).
The Aldine Adagia (1508)
The Adagia — a collection of classical proverbs with commentary — had first appeared in Paris in 1500 with about 800 entries. The Venetian edition, published by Aldus in September 1508, expanded the work to 3,260 proverbs, nearly four times the size of its predecessor (Lowry, p. 242, n. 42). This publication “saw the definite transformation of Erasmus from a promising minor author to an international literary figure” (Lowry, p. 242). The work became a European bestseller, ran through numerous editions, and did much to spread the Aldine reputation across the continent.
Life in the Aldine Workshop
Erasmus lived and worked in the Torresani household (Aldus’ partner Andrea Torresani of Asola, whose daughter Maria Aldus had married). Lowry provides a vivid account of the conditions:

“In 1508 Erasmus sat in one corner of the printing room, writing the Adagia from memory and handing his text sheet by sheet to the compositors, too busy, by his own account, to scratch his ears. In another corner sat Aldus, quietly reading over the proofs and countering all pleas that they had been checked already with the words ‘I’m studying’. Between them the types rattled in the hands of the compositors, and ink was daubed over anything that happened to be in the way, until far into the night, while the Dutchman’s stomach, unused to this pressure of work on short commons, rumbled in ever increasing protest” (Lowry, p. 109).

Erasmus spoke of a household of some thirty people, including workmen, servants, the family, and eight or nine guests — “a now almost incredible mixture of the sweatshop, the boarding house, and the research institute” (Lowry, pp. 109, 113).
Opulentia Sordida
Years later, after Erasmus had been attacked by several Italians for alleged ingratitude to Aldus and gluttony during his stay, he replied in 1531 with the biting dialogue Opulentia Sordida (“How to be rich without showing it”). The piece features “Gilbert” (Erasmus) returning from “Synodium” (Venice), his wan appearance explained by the rigorous life in the workshop of “Antronius” (Torresani) and his son-in-law “Orthrogonus” (Aldus). Erasmus claimed there had been nothing to eat in the Torresani household anyway, and described how Antronius economised on fuel by grubbing up sodden roots for the fire, served shellfish from the public latrines and minestra made with ancient cheese-rinds, while piling ducats onto his massive fortune (Lowry, pp. 76–77). The real target was Torresani, not Aldus — Orthrogonus is portrayed as industrious and sympathetic but entirely under his father-in-law’s thumb (Lowry, p. 77).
Relationship with Aldus
Despite the later satire aimed at Torresani, Erasmus always retained the highest respect for Aldus himself. In the Adagia he paid a famous tribute to the printer, and in The Praise of Folly (written just after leaving Italy) he light-heartedly joked about Aldus’ obsession with grammatical accuracy, crediting him with five grammars (Lowry, p. 62). Lowry notes that “Erasmus’ famous tribute in the Adagia has been mentioned many times … There is no doubt that constant repetitions of that passage have done much to fix the printer’s reputation in the minds of posterity” (Lowry, p. 242). Erasmus also worked during his Venetian stay on an edition of Terence that was eventually printed by Torresani in 1517 (Lowry, p. 262).
Impact and Legacy
The 1508 Aldine Adagia transformed Erasmus from a promising scholar into Europe’s most celebrated living author. For the Aldine Press, it was one of “a number of unquestionably successful popular works, such as Bembo’s Asolani and Erasmus’ Adagia” (Lowry, p. 148). The collaboration demonstrated the Aldine model at its best: a learned author working shoulder-to-shoulder with a scholar-printer, producing a work that combined philological rigour with broad commercial appeal. Erasmus’ Venetian connection, though lasting only months, was arguably the most consequential single visit by any Northern humanist to the Republic, and it forged a lasting link between the Aldine Press and the Northern Renaissance.

entities/fondaco-dei-tedeschi.title: Fondaco dei Tedeschi
entities/fondaco-dei-tedeschi.content:
Fondaco dei Tedeschi

The Fondaco dei Tedeschi’s position next to the Rialto Bridge on the Grand Canal. The schematic shows the Fondaco (orange) on the north side of the canal, directly across from the Rialto market and banking district — the most prominent of Venice’s foreign trading compounds, where German merchants lived, stored goods, and transacted business under strict state regulation.
The Fondaco dei Tedeschi (German Warehouse) was the combined lodging-house, warehouse, and trading post for German merchants in Venice, situated on the Grand Canal next to the Rialto Bridge. It was the most important single node in the overland trade route that connected Venice with Central Europe — the economic lifeline that brought silver and copper from the German mines and carried Venetian spices, silks, and Eastern goods back across the Alps. The Fondaco was much more than a building: it was the institutional heart of the German presence in Venice, a state-controlled monopoly that funnelled the entire overland trade through one point where it could be taxed, monitored, and directed.

Location and Construction
The Fondaco was built on the Grand Canal, directly adjacent to the Rialto Bridge, at the very heart of Venice’s commercial district. The site was chosen deliberately: the Rialto was the city’s wholesale market, and the Fondaco’s position gave German merchants immediate access to the bankers, brokers, and shippers who gathered there.
Lane records that the Venetian government began in 1228 to build the Fondaco for the German merchants (Lane, p. 61). The building was enlarged and rebuilt several times over the centuries; the present structure, which now houses a luxury department store, dates largely from a 16th-century reconstruction after a fire in 1505.

State Control and Regulation
The Fondaco dei Tedeschi was a state-controlled institution. The Venetian government owned the building and regulated every aspect of the Germans’ commercial activity within it. Germans were required to lodge and store their goods there — they could not rent private accommodation or warehouses elsewhere in the city (Lane, p. 61).
This system served several purposes. It allowed the government to monitor and tax all German trade efficiently. It prevented German merchants from establishing independent commercial networks within the city. And it provided the Germans with secure, well-regulated facilities in a foreign city where they might otherwise be vulnerable.
Lane notes that Germans “were forbidden to ship their wares overseas from Venice” — the overland trade was one thing, but the maritime trade was reserved for Venetian merchants. What the Germans wanted, primarily, was to sell their metals and manufactured goods in Venice and to obtain “a wide choice of products to take back across the Alps” (Lane, p. 61).

The German Trade
The Germans were the most important group of foreign merchants in Venice. Their trade route came down from the Brenner Pass to Verona, then continued down the Adige River to its mouth in the Adriatic, where canals connected it to the Venetian lagoon (Lane, p. 61). This was the shortest and most practical route from Central Europe to the Mediterranean.
The goods the Germans brought were mainly metals — silver, copper, iron — from the rich mines of Bohemia, Saxony, and the Tyrol. They also brought cloth, furs, and manufactured goods. In return, they carried away spices, silk, cotton, dyestuffs, and other Eastern luxury goods that had arrived in Venice via the Mediterranean trade. The exchange was fundamental to both economies: the German mines supplied Venice with the silver that was the basis of its coinage, while Venice supplied Germany with the products of the Orient.

The Banking Connection: Silver, Credit, and Exchange
The Fondaco was not merely a warehouse but the gateway for the silver and copper that powered the Venetian mint and the entire system of Venetian exchange. German merchants were the largest single suppliers of bullion to Venice’s mints, and their arrival at the Fondaco with shipments of silver and copper coins was a recurring event in the life of the Rialto banking district.
The Venetian Silver Office (Ufficio dell’Argento) competed with other buyers to purchase from the German importers, and the exchange of coins with German customers was a major line of business for Venetian bankers. Bankers such as Cristoforo Zancani, known to have had close ties with German importers from Nuremberg, specialised in the exchange of coins in large quantities with German customers (Mueller, pp. 8930-8938). The Fondaco itself gave its name to the standard measure of silver shipments: the Latin phrase in milliaribus fontici Teutonicorum (“in the hundredweights of the Fondaco dei Tedeschi”) appears in mint accounts as the standard unit for recording German bullion imports (Mueller, p. 6583).
The relationship between German suppliers and Venetian banks was not simply one of buyer and seller; it was a credit relationship. Bankers were the “immediate suppliers of coin” for German trade, extending credit terms so that German importers could pay over time for the goods they purchased. The connection was deep enough that when a bank failed, German creditors were among those caught — one German creditor of a failed bank blurted out the news “at the request of the city council of Nuremberg,” indicating that the Nuremberg city government took a direct interest in the solvency of Venetian banks where its merchants had deposits (Mueller, pp. 10936-10996).
By the late 15th and early 16th centuries, German merchant-banking companies had grown to the scale where they rivalled Venetian firms. The Fugger family of Augsburg — the most powerful banking house in Europe — established operations in Venice. Along with copper and silver, the Fugger connection brought something else through the Fondaco: “the movable type of a” printing press (Mueller, p. 12082, text cut off), linking the German trade not only to Venetian finance but to the birth of the printed book.

The Book Trade: Aldine Books Across the Alps
The Fondaco dei Tedeschi became a conduit for one of Venice’s most important cultural exports: the printed book. Aldus Manutius, whose Aldine Press was located a short walk from the Fondaco, distributed many of his books to Germany through the German merchants who lodged there (Lowry, p. 3939). The overland route that brought German silver south carried Aldine octavos — the first portable editions of the Greek classics — back north across the Alps.
This was not incidental. The German market was crucial to Aldus’s business model. His small, affordable octavo editions were designed for precisely the kind of reader who could carry them in a saddlebag across the Brenner Pass. The Fondaco merchants, who already managed the logistics of transporting heavy goods in both directions, were natural distributors for books as well.
The connection went both ways: one of Aldus’s collaborators is recorded as having “distributed many of his books to Germany,” and Italian printers in general looked to the German lands as a market for their learned editions (Lowry, pp. 1564, 3939). The Fondaco was the physical node through which the printed word, like the silver coin and the bale of pepper, travelled between Venice and Central Europe.

The Bridge Over the Grand Canal
The Fondaco’s position next to the Rialto Bridge was no accident. The bridge — first a wooden pontoon bridge, then a permanent wooden structure, and finally the stone bridge built between 1588 and 1591 — connected the Fondaco directly to the Rialto marketplace on the other side of the Grand Canal (Lane, p. 14).
This bridge was the only dry crossing of the Grand Canal in the heart of the city until the 19th century, making the Fondaco dei Tedeschi and the Rialto market effectively a single commercial complex. German merchants could cross from their lodgings to the banks, the exchanges, and the wholesale market without setting foot in a boat.

The German “Nation”
The German merchants in Venice were not an unorganised crowd. They belonged to what contemporaries called the Nazione Tedesca — a recognised community with its own internal hierarchy, customs, and representative structures. The city governments of German towns, particularly Nuremberg, took an active interest in the welfare of their merchants in Venice and corresponded with the Venetian government on their behalf.
The Venetian state enforced strict limits on the German community: Germans were confined to the Fondaco, subjected to curfews, and prohibited from conducting retail trade or shipping goods overseas. But within these constraints, the German “nation” operated as a cohesive commercial community, bound by shared language, law, and credit networks. The Fondaco had its own chapel, its own internal regulations, and its own elected officers who mediated disputes and represented the community to the Venetian authorities.

Later History
The Fondaco dei Tedeschi continued to function as a German trading post through the 16th and 17th centuries, though its importance declined as the Atlantic trade routes shifted the centre of European commerce away from the Mediterranean, and as the Fuggers and other German banking houses began to deal directly with the Spanish and Portuguese rather than through Venice.
Political disruptions also took their toll. The Emperor Sigismund’s conflicts with Venice at times made it difficult for German merchants to reach the city (Mueller, p. 9697). The changing patterns of European trade after the discovery of the Americas and the Portuguese Cape route redrew the commercial map in ways that marginalised the old Venetian-German axis.
The building was damaged by fire in 1505 and rebuilt in the early 16th century with external frescoes by Giorgione and Titian — the frescoes are now lost to the elements, but fragments and copies survive. After the fall of the Republic in 1797, the Fondaco passed through various uses — customs house, tobacco factory, and eventually, in the 20th century, the central post office of Venice. It was restored in the 2010s and reopened as a luxury department store, its commercial purpose intact if transformed.

entities/fra-mauro.title: Fra Mauro
entities/fra-mauro.content:
Fra Mauro
Fra Mauro (c. 1400–1459) was a Camaldolite monk and the greatest European cartographer of the 15th century. His world map of 1459 — the Mappa Mundi — is the most detailed and accurate map of the known world produced before the Age of Discovery. Created in his workshop on the island of Murano in the Venetian lagoon, it synthesised information from classical geography (Ptolemy), medieval travel narratives (Marco Polo and the milione tradition), contemporary portolan charts, and direct reports from merchants and navigators across three continents. Fra Mauro was not a great explorer himself — he never left the lagoon — but he was the most accomplished synthesiser of geographical knowledge that Europe had yet produced.
The Camaldolite Order and the Murano Workshop
Fra Mauro lived and worked in the monastery of San Michele in Isola on Murano, the glass-making island north of Venice. The Camaldolites (Camaldolesi) were a reformed Benedictine order — ascetic, scholarly, and intellectual — whose houses were centres of manuscript copying and scholarly work. San Michele in Isola was precisely the kind of institution where a monk of scholarly inclinations could assemble a library, receive visitors, and correspond with geographers, merchants, and navigators from across Europe.
His monastery became a centre of cartographic production. Lane describes his workshop as one that “combined the methods and information of the chart makers with what could be learned from scholars” (Lane, p. 278). Mauro employed assistants — the most notable being Andrea Bianco, himself a noted cartographer and a navigation officer on Venetian galley fleets, who contributed direct maritime knowledge of the Atlantic and African coasts. The workshop produced multiple copies of maps on commission; the Mappa Mundi was the culmination of decades of cartographic work.
Mauro was not merely a compiler. He was a critical geographer who weighed sources against each other and made deliberate judgments about which reports to trust. When Ptolemy’s recently rediscovered Geographia (Γεωγραφικὴ Ὑφήγησις) contradicted the reports of contemporary travellers, Mauro often preferred the modern accounts — a strikingly empirical approach for his time. He was willing to tell Ptolemy he was wrong, and to say so explicitly in the inscriptions on his map.
The Portolan Chart Tradition
Fra Mauro’s work stood at the intersection of two traditions of geographical representation: the mappamundi (schematic world maps, usually centred on Jerusalem, organised around biblical geography) and the carta portolana (carta nautica — nautical chart). The portolan charts were practical instruments: they showed accurate coastal outlines, marked harbours and hazards, and were used by navigators at sea. Venetian and Genoese navigators had been producing them since the late thirteenth century, and by Fra Mauro’s time they covered the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, and the Atlantic coasts of Europe and Africa with remarkable precision.
Fra Mauro incorporated the portolan chart’s precise coastlines into a world-map framework, giving his Mappa Mundi an accuracy of coastal outline that the mappamundi tradition had never achieved. At the same time, he retained the mappamundi’s ambition to represent the entire known world — not just the navigable coasts but the interiors of Asia, Africa, and the mythological regions beyond.
The Mappa Mundi (1459): Key Features
Fra Mauro’s great world map was completed in 1459, commissioned by King Afonso V of Portugal. It is a circular map about two metres (passi) in diameter, drawn on vellum (pergamena) and illuminated in gold, red, blue, and green. It is now preserved in the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana in Venice.
Key features:
Accurate coastlines: Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Black Sea are drawn with remarkable accuracy based on portolan charts and the direct reports of Venetian and Genoese navigators. Italy, the Iberian Peninsula, and the Levantine coast are recognisably modern in outline.
Africa as circumnavigable: Fra Mauro’s map shows Africa as a landmass with a sea route around its southern tip — decades before Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. This was not guesswork: Mauro had received reports from Ethiopian travellers (Etiopi) who described the southern limits of the continent, and from Venetian merchants and navigators who had explored the African coast. He noted explicitly on the map that an Arab ship had supposedly rounded the southern cape and sailed into the “Sea of India” — a report he did not fully believe but could not ignore.
The interior of Asia and Africa: Unlike most earlier maps, which left continental interiors blank or filled them with mythological creatures (cynocephalae, dog-headed men; blemmyae, men with faces on their chests), Mauro’s map includes detailed topographical information — river systems, mountain ranges, cities, and trade routes drawn from the reports of merchants and travellers, including those who had traversed the Silk Road in the era of the Pax Mongolica.
The Indian Ocean: Fra Mauro showed the Indian Ocean as an open sea connected to the Atlantic — rejecting Ptolemy’s claim that Africa extended southward indefinitely to join a land barrier enclosing the Indian Ocean as an inland sea. This rejection of Ptolemy was Fra Mauro’s most consequential geographical judgment: it opened the conceptual space for the Cape route.
Southern orientation: The map is oriented with south at the top — following a convention common in Arabic and medieval cartography (Islamic mapmakers traditionally placed south at the top as a reflection of the Qibla orientation). The effect in modern eyes is disorienting: Europe is at the bottom, Asia at the right, Africa at the top-left.
Inscriptions: The map is covered with hundreds of explanatory iscrizioni (inscriptions) in Venetian dialect and Latin, describing the peoples, products, and politics of each region. These texts reveal Fra Mauro’s sources: Ptolemy, Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta’s Rihla (indirectly), Ethiopian informants, Portuguese navigators, and the accumulated knowledge of Venetian merchants who had traded across the known world.
Venice and Portugal: The Intelligence Connection
The patronage of the Portuguese king was deliberate. Portugal was then the leading edge of the European expansion along the African coast, and Prince Henry the Navigator — the driving force behind Portuguese exploration — had a well-organised intelligence operation that sought geographical information wherever it could be found. Prince Peter (Dom Pedro), Henry’s brother, visited Fra Mauro in Murano and commissioned a world map for the Portuguese project of African exploration.
Fra Mauro and Andrea Bianco produced this copy, which was delivered to Portugal just before Fra Mauro’s death in 1459 (Lane, p. 278). The relationship between Venetian cartography and Portuguese exploration was part of a larger pattern: Venetian mapmakers, using information gathered by Venetian merchants across three continents, supplied Portuguese navigators with some of the best geographical knowledge available. The Cape route was built, in part, on Venetian geographical intelligence gathered at Aden, Ormuz, Tana, Trebizond, and Alexandria — and synthesised in Fra Mauro’s workshop on Murano.
The Paradox of Fra Mauro’s Legacy
Fra Mauro’s map was both the culmination of pre-Columbian cartography and the instrument of its own obsolescence. Within a generation of its completion, Bartolomeu Dias (1488), Vasco da Gama (1498), and Columbus (1492) transformed the European understanding of the world’s geography so completely that Fra Mauro’s framework — however sophisticated and empirical by the standards of his time — was rendered a historical artifact.
His workshop on Murano was a distinctly Venetian institution: a place where scholarly and practical knowledge met, where the classical inheritance was tested against the reports of merchants and sailors, and where the results were captured in maps that circulated to the courts of Europe. It exemplifies the Venetian capacity to integrate learning and commerce — the same capacity that made the Aldine Press, the Procurators’ archive, and the merchant-banker partnerships of the Rialto all characteristic expressions of the same culture.

entities/francesco-foscari.title: Francesco Foscari
entities/francesco-foscari.content:
Francesco Foscari
Francesco Foscari (1373–1457) was Doge of Venice from 1423 to 1457 — the longest dogeship of any 15th-century doge, spanning thirty-four years of almost continuous warfare. His reign marked Venice’s decisive turn toward territorial expansion on the Italian mainland (terraferma), a policy that brought vast conquests but ultimately ended in personal and political tragedy. His story is the subject of Byron’s play The Two Foscari and Verdi’s opera I due Foscari, and his figure represents the most historically contested dogeship of the Renaissance: the man who made Venice a great power in Italy, at the cost of its maritime identity.
The Mocenigo Warning and the Election of 1423
Foscari was elected doge in 1423 against the explicit warning of the dying Doge Tommaso Mocenigo. Mocenigo’s “Farewell Address” — delivered on his deathbed and recorded by chroniclers as the most famous political speech in Venetian history — was a detailed economic argument for caution. Mocenigo described Venice’s current prosperity in quantitative terms: the public debt was being reduced, commerce was flourishing, the city was peaceful. He then named the men most likely to succeed him and explained why each was unsuitable. Of Foscari specifically: “he spreads lies and other statements without foundation and swoops and soars more than a hawk or falcon. And if you make him doge, which God forbid, you will shortly be at war” (Lane, pp. 228–229).
Foscari was elected nonetheless, and within months Venice was at war with Milan. The Mocenigo warning was remembered for centuries as prophetic.
Lane observes that the issue separating Foscari from Mocenigo was not simply sea versus land, or caution versus aggression. Foscari was equally assertive in both theatres: immediately after becoming doge, he accepted the offer of Salonica (Thessalonike — the second city of Byzantium) from the Byzantine Emperor and sent a fleet under Pietro Loredan to defend it (Lane, p. 229). Venice held Salonica for seven years against Ottoman pressure before selling it back to the Byzantines in 1430 — a calculation, not a capitulation. The more fundamental division was between Mocenigo’s belief that Venice’s wealth was best sustained by commercial peace, and Foscari’s conviction that Venice could only maintain its position by dominating its immediate Italian environment.
Mainland Expansion: The Wars with Milan
Under Foscari’s leadership, Venice pursued an aggressive programme of territorial expansion in Lombardy. The principal theatre was the war against Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan — the dominant power of northern Italy and Venice’s most dangerous neighbour. Venice allied with Florence (which shared Venice’s interest in containing Milanese expansion), hired major condottieri including Francesco Bussone (Carmagnola) and Erasmo da Narni (Gattamelata), and fought a series of campaigns that by the 1440s had brought Brescia (1426), Bergamo (1428), Crema (1449), and much of the surrounding countryside under Venetian control (Lane, pp. 229–234).
The terraferma empire that emerged from these wars — stretching from Udine in the north to Brescia in the west and Ravenna in the south — was the largest continuous territorial possession Venice would ever hold. It gave the Republic access to grain, timber, and the Alpine passes that fed trade from Germany; it also gave it a land frontier to defend and a military apparatus to maintain.
Lane describes Foscari as “the leader of the Venetian ‘hawks’” (Lane, p. 267) — a man who dominated the Venetian councils through three decades of war by the force of his personality and his ability to command majorities in the Great Council. His portrait by Lazzaro Bastiani (Figure 19 in Lane, p. 231), now in the Museo Correr, shows the imperious expression of a man accustomed to power: the corno (ducal horn) set at a precise angle, the eyes fixed, the bearing that of a man who would not easily yield. Foscari was the first doge since the constitutional reforms of the 13th century to exert genuine personal leadership in formulating and executing policy (Lane, p. 267).
The Cost of War: Public Debt and Tax Burden
The cost of these mainland wars was enormous. The Venetian state financed warfare primarily through forced loans (prestiti) levied on the property of the nobility and citizenry — loans in theory, but in practice taxes, since the bonds (Monte Vecchio and Monte Nuovo) issued in exchange paid interest at well below market rates and were often permanently devalued. By the 1450s, after three decades of intermittent war, the public debt had soared to levels that alarmed the patriciate. Lane notes that direct income taxes — the decima (ten percent of income) and other levies — were adopted to supplement the forced loan system, a fiscal innovation that reflected the inadequacy of traditional methods (Lane, p. 259).
War taxes became a bitter burden, and the territorial conquests — however impressive — were purchased at the price of overextending the Republic’s financial and demographic resources. The same generation of Venetian nobles who accumulated the terraferma also saw the price of government bonds fall catastrophically as the state serviced its debt by debasement and deferred payment. The tension between the beneficiaries of expansion (those with mainland estates and offices) and those who bore the cost (holders of depreciating bonds, merchants whose capital was drained by forced loans) was a constant undercurrent of Foscari-era politics.
The Condottieri System
The wars were fought primarily through hired professional soldiers — condottieri (condottiero, singular) — and the armies they commanded. The condotta was a contract specifying the number of lance (mounted cavalry units) or fanti (infantry) the condottiere would furnish, the term of service, and the payment. The state paid; the condottiere recruited, trained, and commanded. The system gave Venice military capability without requiring it to transform its citizenry into soldiers — a fundamental Venetian preference — but it also created the dependency, the vulnerability to betrayal, and the difficulty of holding condottieri to aggressive action that characterised Venetian land warfare throughout the period.
Carmagnola (Francesco Bussone) was the first great condottiere of the Foscari era, whose unexplained hesitation at Soncino in 1431 led the Council of Ten to accuse him of treachery; he was tried and executed in 1432, the victim of a system in which suspicion of condottieri was endemic. Gattamelata (Erasmo da Narni), by contrast, served Venice loyally until his death in 1443 and was honoured with Donatello’s equestrian statue in Padua — the first such monument to a non-sovereign commander since antiquity.
The Tragedy of Jacopo Foscari
Foscari’s downfall was precipitated by the processus (legal proceedings) against his son, Jacopo Foscari. Jacopo was twice accused of corruption and treasonable correspondence with foreign princes — first with the Duke of Milan, then with the Ottoman Sultan. He was tortured, exiled to Nauplion in Greece, recalled, tortured again, and sent into a second exile at Crete, where he died. The conflict between the doge’s paternal affections and his obligation under Venetian constitutional norms to recuse himself from proceedings involving his own family became a causa celebre (causa notoria) — a public scandal discussed throughout Europe.
The truth of the accusations against Jacopo has never been established with certainty. What is clear is that the proceedings were used by the doge’s enemies — primarily the Loredan faction, whose enmity toward the Foscari went back to the death of a Loredan in Venetian service, whom the Loredan family blamed on Foscari’s war policy — to destabilise the doge politically. When the expansion in Lombardy was checked by the rise of Francesco Sforza (who made himself Duke of Milan in 1450 and negotiated the Peace of Lodi with Venice in 1454), when war taxes had become unbearable, and when Foscari was made politically vulnerable by Jacopo’s repeated misconduct, his enemies struck.
In 1457, after thirty-four years in office, “the proud, imperious Francesco Foscari was deposed by vote of the Ducal Councillors and the Ten, led by a Loredan” (Lane, p. 267). He died a few days later — according to tradition, upon hearing the bell of San Marco announce his successor’s election. The deposition was unprecedented: no doge had been deposed since the constitutional reforms of the 13th century.
Lane contrasts Foscari’s spirited response to military defeat — appearing before the councils “confidently dressed in his most gorgeous golden robes” after battlefield reverses — with the despondent behaviour of later doges like Leonardo Loredan after Agnadello (Lane, p. 270). The contrast illuminates the difference between a doge who wielded genuine power and one who served primarily as a constitutional figurehead.
Ca’ Foscari and Architectural Legacy
During his dogeship, Foscari built the Ca’ Foscari palace on the Grand Canal — the grandest private Gothic palace in Venice. Its facade, with its multiple orders of Gothic windows and its expansive piano nobile (principal floor), expressed the wealth and ambition of the Foscari family at their height. The building now houses the University of Venice, which has taken the name Ca’ Foscari University — an ironic memorial to the man whose deposition it commemorates.
Assessment
Foscari’s long dogeship was a watershed in Venetian history. He committed Venice to the path of mainland empire that would define its politics for the next 250 years — a path from which it could not retreat, even when the costs became clear. The terraferma empire generated revenues, provided strategic depth, and gave the Republic the resources to sustain its maritime operations. But it also diverted resources from the Aegean and Ionian bases that were being progressively overwhelmed by Ottoman power — and it required Venice to compete on the Italian mainland against opponents whose land armies were, in the end, larger than Venice’s hired forces could match.
The debate between Mocenigo’s caution and Foscari’s assertiveness — sea versus land, commercial peace versus territorial expansion — would echo through Venetian councils for generations. Neither position was simply right or wrong; the Republic needed both commercial access and territorial security. Foscari’s tragedy was that he pursued territorial expansion with a single-mindedness that sacrificed the financial moderation and political consensus on which the Venetian system depended.

entities/francesco-griffo.title: Francesco Griffo (Francesco da Bologna)
entities/francesco-griffo.content:
Francesco Griffo (Francesco da Bologna)
Francesco Griffo (also known as Francesco da Bologna) was the most accomplished punchcutter and type designer of the early Aldine Press, active in Venice from the early 1490s until about 1502. He designed and cut virtually all of Aldus Manutius’s type-founts — including the first italic type (1501), the roman used for the Hypnerotomachia Polifili (1499), and multiple Greek cursive founts. His work defined the typographic aesthetic of the Aldine Press and, through the italic in particular, influenced book design across Europe for centuries.
Life
Very little is known of Griffo’s early life. He was from Bologna — hence his alternative name “Francesco da Bologna” — and was almost certainly a trained goldsmith or metalworker before turning to punchcutting. Lowry notes that there are “only three fixed points from which we can investigate Francesco’s connection with Venetian printing” (p. 108):

The three-line tribute (terzain) added by Aldus to the first text printed in italic cursive, the Virgil of 1501.
The claim made two years later by Gerolamo Soncino of Fano, that he had secured the services of the expert who had cut all Aldus’s types.
The repetition of that claim by Francesco himself, in an edition of Petrarch’s Canzonieri which he published independently in 1516.

His connection with Aldus lasted ten or twelve years at most, and for only seven of these was the Aldine publishing company in active production (p. 109).
Death
After leaving Aldus, Griffo attempted independent work as a publisher-printer. The strains of independent action appear to have been too great. Lowry records that “shortly afterwards he brained his son-in-law with an iron bar — perhaps an incomplete type punch — faced a murder-charge in Bologna with unknown results, and sank into an obscurity from which the most searching efforts of scholarship have still failed to rouse him” (p. 108). According to Mardersteig (cited in Lowry’s note 70), the attack on his son-in-law occurred in May 1518, and by October 1519 Francesco was referred to as deceased.
Work for Aldus Manutius
The Roman Type for Hypnerotomachia Polifili (1499)
Griffo cut the roman type used for the celebrated Hypnerotomachia Polifili, the elaborate allegorical romance printed in December 1499. This was Aldus’s most visually ambitious publication, and the type — a refined, open roman — contributed significantly to the book’s reputation as one of the most beautiful printed books of the Renaissance. The same type was also used for other Aldine productions of the period (Lowry, p. 133, note on type of Polifilo).
The First Italic Type (1501)
Griffo’s most famous creation is the Aldine italic, first used for the Virgil of April 1501. The type was based on the cursive chancery hand (cancelleresca) then fashionable among humanist scribes, particularly the style associated with Niccolo Niccoli and later practitioners such as Bartolomeo di San Vito and Antonio de’ Tagliente. Aldus introduced the type with a three-line tribute in Latin elegiac couplets (a terzain) that credits Griffo by name:

Qui Gratis dedit Aldus, en Latinis
Dat nunc grammata scalpta daedaleis
Francisci manibus Bononiensis.

(“Aldus, who gave you Latin texts for nothing, now gives you letters carved by the Daedalean hands of Francesco of Bologna.“)
The italic was not designed — as is often mistakenly assumed — to economise on space by cramming more letters onto each page. Lowry argues convincingly that Aldus’s aim was aesthetic: to give his printed texts the same status and elegance as the most fashionable manuscript books, which had long used the cursive hand. The italic was a continuation of the humanistic Roman style, not a departure from it (pp. 160-161).
Greek Types
Griffo cut four Greek cursive founts for Aldus, each similar in basic conception but differing in detail. These were used for the landmark series of Greek editions — Aristotle, Aristophanes, Sophocles, the Greek dramatists — that formed the core of Aldus’s programme. One of the technical innovations attributed to Griffo is a system of “kerning” accents into the top of vowel sorts, avoiding the awkward overprinting of separate accent pieces (p. 110).
Hebrew Type
Griffo also cut a Hebrew fount for Aldus. Though never applied to the ambitious trilingual Bible projects Aldus planned, it was used sporadically throughout his lifetime (p. 109).
Twelve Type-Founts in Three Languages
Altogether, during his association with Aldus, Griffo cut twelve type-founts: six rounded (Roman) Latin types, the famous italic, four Greek cursives, and one Hebrew fount. Lowry writes: “When we speak of Aldine typography, we are speaking of Griffo’s workmanship” (p. 109). After Griffo’s departure in 1502, no new type designs were introduced by the Aldine Press.
The Dispute over Credit
The relationship between Aldus and Griffo ended in acrimony. Griffo’s departure from Venice late in 1502 coincides closely with Aldus’s grant of a comprehensive monopoly (14 November 1502) over all Greek publication and all Latin printing in italic within the Venetian dominions.
Gerolamo Soncino explicitly charged that Aldus and others had usurped the credit for inventions made by Griffo, whom he described as “a most excellent cutter of Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters, a man whose genius finds no equal in this craft” (p. 108). The contradiction between Aldus’s claims in his petitions for privilege — that he had “discovered two new methods” or “devised a new kind of letter called cursive” — and the counterclaims of Soncino and Griffo himself could not be resolved in the legal framework of the time, which protected only the investor, not the craftsman (pp. 109-111).
Lowry suggests that the breach was less a matter of personal clash than of changing commercial structures. Aldus was moving away from hands-on technical involvement toward organisation and public relations, while Griffo belonged to the older world of the master-craftsman who directed every stage of production. “When men of such wildly different background and commitment as these last two were doing the same job, and when the concept of a specialised service-industry had yet to emerge, it was almost inevitable that a man like Griffo would get hurt” (p. 111).
Work after Aldus: Gerson Soncino
After leaving Aldus, Griffo worked for Gerolamo (Gerson) Soncino, a Jewish printer active in Fano. If Griffo designed and cut the punches for Aldus’s last distinct type (the small Greek cursive for Sophocles, August 1502), then equipped Soncino with a Latin italic fount in time for an edition by 7 July 1503, the signs are that he left Venice late in 1502 (p. 109).
Independent Printing
In 1516, Griffo published his own edition of Petrarch’s Canzonieri, in which he repeated the claim that he, not Aldus, deserved the credit for the Aldine types. This venture appears to have been a financial and personal failure. Soon afterward came the murder of his son-in-law and his disappearance from the historical record.
Legacy
Despite his obscurity — no portrait, no surviving correspondence, only a handful of documentary references — Francesco Griffo’s influence on Western typography is incalculable:

The Aldine italic, cut in 1501, became the model for virtually all italic types that followed. It was imitated within years by printers in Lyon, Florence, and elsewhere, and its basic form remains in use today.
The roman type of the Hypnerotomachia Polifili is regarded as one of the finest of the incunable period.
His Greek types set the standard for printing classical texts for decades, and the technical innovation of kerning accents shows his practical ingenuity.

Lowry’s judgment is definitive: “Experiment ended with Griffo’s departure” from the Aldine Press (p. 109).

entities/genoa.title: Genoa
entities/genoa.content:
Genoa

Genoa’s position relative to the Venetian muda convoy routes. The map shows Genoa on the Italian coast west of Venice — Venice’s great maritime rival for control of the Eastern Mediterranean. The contrasting route networks illustrate how the two republics competed for the same trade: spices, silks, and slaves from the Levant.
Genoa was Venice’s great maritime rival in the Mediterranean, the only Italian maritime republic that matched Venice in naval power, commercial reach, and colonial ambition. Their repeated wars for control of Eastern trade routes culminated in the War of Chioggia (1378-81), after which Genoese naval power was permanently broken and Venice emerged as the unchallenged queen of the Eastern Mediterranean.
Maritime Rival
Both republics competed fiercely for the trade of the Levant, the Black Sea, and the Byzantine world. Genoa’s Ligurian littoral, cut off from its hinterland by steep mountains, forced its merchants to look to the sea just as Venice’s lagoon did (Lane, pp. 4245-4249). But Genoa was never as unified a city-state as Venice: factional rivalry between the great families — the Doria, Spinola, and Grimaldi — was more implacable, and control of the communal government frequently passed violently from one group to another, with the defeated sent into exile (Lane, pp. 4253-4259).
Despite having less than half Venice’s population, Genoa grew rapidly between 1100 and 1250 and established at least nominal control over the entire Ligurian coast. Genoese fleets supported the Crusaders more vigorously than Venice did in the 12th century, winning extensive commercial rights in Syrian ports such as Acre and Tyre (Lane, pp. 2089-2092, 4260-4263).
Wars with Venice
The rivalry produced four major wars. The First Genoese War (1256-70) was triggered by a brawl in Acre; a Venetian fleet under Lorenzo Tiepolo defeated the Genoese off Acre in 1258, capturing their ships and settling the dispute in Venice’s favour (Lane, pp. 4277-4319). The Second Genoese War (1294-99) ended inconclusively after the Venetian defeat at Curzola, but the Third Genoese War (1350-55) saw Venice recover from a defeat at Porto Longo through skilled diplomacy, taking advantage of Genoa’s internal divisions (Lane, pp. 9623-9634).
The fourth and climactic war was the War of Chioggia (1378-81). Genoa, allied with the King of Hungary, captured the fishing port of Chioggia at the southern entrance to the Venetian lagoon and blockaded Venice itself. Food supplies were cut off, and panic gripped the city. But the Venetians, under the admiral Vettor Pisani, counter-blockaded the Genoese fleet inside the lagoon, starving them into surrender. The fall of Chioggia on 24 June 1380 saved Venice from annihilation (Lane, pp. 188-198; see war-of-chioggia).
Colonial and Trade Competition
Genoa established an extensive network of colonies and trading posts in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Its colony at Pera, in the harbour of Constantinople, flourished after the Fourth Crusade, and the Genoese built a major shipping centre at Kaffa (Caffa) in the Crimea — a trading post used by both Genoese and Venetian merchants (Lane, pp. 4504-4508). It was from Kaffa that the Black Death reached Italy in 1347, carried aboard a Venetian galley (Lane, pp. 1535-1541). The Genoese also held the Aegean island of Chios and competed with Venice for control of the Cyprus route and the spice trade.
Banking and Exchange
Mueller documents significant financial connections between Venice and Genoa. The two cities maintained active exchange markets: Venice quoted exchange rates with Genoa, and the seasonal pattern of those rates is preserved in the Datini archives from 1384 to 1410 (Mueller, Appendix C.1, C.5). The Borromei company’s London branch sat at the head of two exchange triangles — Venice-London-Bruges and Genoa-London-Bruges — circuits that served to keep funds moving through arbitrage. In 1436, the London branch paid drafts arriving from Genoa, settling them in part with new drafts on Genoa and Venice (Mueller, pp. 326-327).
Genoese bankers were active in Constantinople alongside Venetians and Greeks; the banker Toma Spinola, operating in Constantinople in the 1430s, is identified in the ledger of Giacomo Badoer as “surely a Genoese” (Mueller, p. 5104).
After Chioggia: Decline and Spanish Banking
The War of Chioggia broke Genoa’s ability to challenge Venice at sea. In the decades that followed, Genoa “became less and less able to conduct a foreign policy of her own” (Lane, p. 10770). Venice recovered its strength, restored its rule over Dalmatia, and entered the 15th century as the dominant Mediterranean naval power.
Genoa’s commercial genius did not disappear. The Republic turned increasingly to banking and finance, most famously through the Casa di San Giorgio — a state bank established in 1407 that consolidated the public debt and became one of the first public banks in Europe. In the 16th century, Genoese financiers became the bankers to the Spanish crown, managing the flow of American silver through the Spanish Empire. The Genoese admiral Andrea Doria transferred his allegiance to the Emperor Charles V in 1528, bringing Genoese maritime resources into the service of Spain (Lane, pp. 13001-13003).
Venetian Painting in Genoa
Genoese collections held notable works by Venetian painters. Berenson records portraits by Titian in the collection of Prince Giorgio Doria, paintings by Paolo Veronese in the Brignole-Sale collection, and works by Lorenzo Lotto in Genoese churches (Berenson, pp. 3066, 3480, 3619, 4264).

entities/giorgione.title: Giorgione
entities/giorgione.content:
Giorgione
Giorgio da Castelfranco, called Giorgione (1477/78–1510) was the most influential Venetian painter of the early 16th century despite a working life of barely fifteen years. Berenson calls him a pupil of Giovanni Bellini, influenced by Carpaccio (Index), who combined Bellini’s refined feeling and poetry with Carpaccio’s gaiety and love of colour to create a new kind of painting — intimate, lyrical, and perfectly in touch with the ripened spirit of the Renaissance (Section VII).
The Easel Picture
Berenson’s central thesis is that Giorgione created the easel picture — the small, self-sufficient painting made for private enjoyment in a domestic setting rather than for public or ecclesiastical display. Where Bellini’s late works were already moving in this direction — full of subtle, refined poetry expressible in form and colour alone — they were a little too austere and sober for the gay, care-free youth of the time. Carpaccio had the gaiety but painted few easel pictures. Giorgione, starting with the qualities of both as his inheritance, painted pictures so perfectly in touch with the Renaissance that they met with the success which those things only find that at the same moment wake us to the full sense of a need and satisfy it (Section VII).
The Giorgionesque Spirit
Giorgione created a demand — the Giorgionesque — which other painters were forced to supply at the risk of finding no favour (Section VIII). The older painters accommodated themselves as best they could: Catena’s A Warrior Adoring the Infant Christ in the National Gallery is cited by Berenson as a good accessible instance of the Giorgionesque way of treating a subject — not for the story, nor for display of skill, nor for obvious feeling, but for the lovely landscape, the effects of light and colour, and the sweetness of human relations (Section VIII). Giorgione’s own altar-piece at Castelfranco is treated in precisely the same spirit, but with far more genius.
The Giorgionesque spirit also transformed portraiture. Berenson notes that where earlier portraits like Mantegna’s Scarampo tyrannised the viewer, Giorgione and his followers painted men and women whose very look leads one to think of sympathetic friends — people with pleasantly rounded features, soft raiment, and surroundings that call up the memory of sweet landscapes and refreshing breezes (Section IX).
Major Works
Berenson’s index records the following works as by Giorgione:

Castelfranco Madonna (Duomo, Castelfranco) — Madonna with SS. Francis and Liberale, the supreme example of the Giorgionesque spirit in altar-piece form (Section VIII)
Sleeping Venus (Dresden, 185) — the first reclining female nude in Venetian painting
Fete Champetre (Paris, 1136 — Concert Champetre, now widely attributed to Titian)
The Three Philosophers (Vienna, 16 — listed as “Evander showing Aeneas the Site of Rome”)
Trial of Moses and Judgment of Solomon (Florence, Uffizi, 621, 630)
Gipsy and Soldier (Venice, Giovanelli collection — possibly a version of the Tempest)
Portrait of Antonio Brocardo (Buda-Pesth, 94)
Portrait of a Lady (Rome, Villa Borghese, 143)
Christ Bearing the Cross (Vicenza, Casa Loschi; and Venice, S. Rocco)
Storm Calmed by St. Mark (Venice, Academy, 516 — finished in small part by Paris Bordone)
Apollo and Daphne (Venice, Seminario)

The Tempest (Venice, Accademia), now one of Giorgione’s most celebrated works, is not listed by Berenson under that title; his “Gipsy and Soldier” at the Giovanelli collection may correspond to the same subject.
Influence on Titian
Giorgione’s closest follower was the young Titian, with whom he worked on the external frescoes of the Fondaco dei Tedeschi at the Rialto (c.1508–9, now almost entirely lost). Berenson writes that Titian, in spite of a sturdier, less refined nature, did nothing for a generation after Giorgione’s death but work on his lines — his early pictures have not only many of Giorgione’s qualities but something more, as if done by an older Giorgione with better possession of himself and a larger hold on the world (Section X).
Death and Legacy
Giorgione died in Venice in 1510 during the plague, aged only about 33. Fewer than a score of his works have survived destruction, but these suffice, Berenson says, to give a glimpse into that brief moment when the Renaissance found its most genuine expression in painting. His works continue to be appreciated most by people whose attitude of mind and spirit has most in common with that period (Section VII).
Berenson’s Assessment

“His pictures are the perfect reflex of the Renaissance at its height.” — Berenson, Section VII

Berenson adds that the Renaissance has the fascination of youth — those years when we seemed so full of promise both to ourselves and to everybody else (Section VIII). Few painters capture that quality as fully as Giorgione.
The mystery of Giorgione remains: very few works are universally authenticated, and attributions have been fiercely debated for centuries. What is not in doubt is that he invented the easel picture, created the Giorgionesque spirit that dominated Venetian painting for a generation, and through his influence on Titian shaped the entire future of European art.

entities/giovanni-bellini.title: Giovanni Bellini
entities/giovanni-bellini.content:
Giovanni Bellini
Giovanni Bellini (c.1430–1516) was, according to Berenson, “the greatest Venetian master of the fifteenth century” (Berenson, Section II, body lines 444–445). He was the son of Jacopo Bellini (active 1430–1470, a pupil of Gentile da Fabriano and Pisanello) and the brother of Gentile Bellini (1429–1507). Berenson’s catalogue records Giovanni as a pupil of his father Jacopo, formed in Padua under the influence of Donatello (catalogue lines 3401–3402). His brother-in-law was Andrea Mantegna, whose sculptural linearism influenced Bellini’s early style.
Religious Intensity and the Church
Berenson’s Section II — “The Church and Painting” — singles out Giovanni Bellini as the painter whose early works best fulfil the Church’s religious intention. At a time when painting had overcome the technical obstacles to expressing profound emotion, Bellini’s art became a direct stimulus to devotion: “No one can look at Bellini’s pictures of the Dead Christ upheld by the Virgin or angels without being put into a mood of deep contrition, nor at his earlier Madonnas without a thrill of awe and reverence” (Section II, lines 450–456). His contemporaries — Gentile Bellini, the Vivarini, Crivelli, and Cima da Conegliano — began painting in the same spirit and produced almost the same effect (Section II, lines 457–460).
Pageant Pictures and Public Commissions
In Section V (“Pageant Pictures”), Berenson notes that Giovanni and Gentile Bellini, together with Cima and Carpaccio, were the painters who met with greatest success in solving the problems of narrative painting at the end of the fifteenth century (lines 935–939). The Bellini were employed to execute a second rendering of the historical subjects in the Hall of the Great Council of the Doge’s Palace, giving scope to the Venetian love of processions and civic pageantry (Section V, lines 1055–1064). Gentile Bellini’s Corpus Christi picture and Preaching of St. Mark exemplify this genre, as does his Miracle of the True Cross with its vivid genre episodes of gondoliers, servants, and onlookers (Section VI, lines 1134–1154).
Portraiture
Giovanni and Gentile Bellini also executed portraits of the Doges for the Great Hall. Berenson notes that these portraits “must have had no less influence on portraiture than their mural paintings in the same Hall had on other branches of the art” (Section IX, lines 1566–1571). Among the surviving portraits from the Bellini workshop is Giovanni’s celebrated portrait of Doge Leonardo Loredan (1501, National Gallery, London), listed in the catalogue (line 3408).
Late Style and Easel Pictures
Berenson’s Section VIII observes that some of Giovanni Bellini’s late works are “full of that subtle, refined poetry which can be expressed in form and colour alone” — pictures that “could no more permit being translated into words than a sonata” (lines 1312–1320). Though a little too austere in form and sober in colour for the gay youth of the time, these works paved the way for Giorgione, who “combined the refined feeling and poetry of Bellini with Carpaccio’s gaiety and love of beauty and colour” (Section VIII, lines 1331–1335).
Major Works
The catalogue records Bellini’s principal altar-pieces: the Frari Triptych (Madonna and Saints, 1488), the San Zaccaria Altarpiece (Madonna and four Saints, 1505), the San Giovanni Crisostomo Altarpiece (SS. Jerome, Augustine, and Christopher, 1513), and the San Francesco della Vigna Altarpiece (Madonna and four Saints, 1507). Among his devotional works are the Pietà in the Brera, the Transfiguration in Naples, the Baptism in S. Corona, Vicenza (1510), and the Agony in the Garden in the National Gallery, London (catalogue lines 3404–3451). His late Allegories in the Venice Academy reveal the reflective, poetic quality Berenson admired.
Workshop and Influence
Bellini ran a large workshop. The catalogue lists Bissolo (1464–1528) as “pupil and assistant of Giovanni Bellini” (line 3474) and Giovanni Busi, called Cabiani (c.1480–1544) as pupil of Bellini and Palma (line 3768). Sebastiano del Piombo “had learned to paint under Bellini, Cima, and Giorgione” (Section XVI, line 2058). Most importantly, both Giorgione and Titian began their careers in Bellini’s orbit. Titian, the central figure of 16th-century Venetian painting, trained under Bellini before emerging in the circle of Giorgione.
Berenson’s Assessment and Legacy
For Berenson, Giovanni Bellini stands at the threshold of the Venetian Renaissance. His early religious works represent the highest fulfilment of the Church’s didactic and devotional aims in painting, while his late works anticipate the autonomous, poetic easel picture perfected by Giorgione. Bellini’s career spans the transition from the austere piety of the early Quattrocento to the full humanism of the High Renaissance. He died in Venice in 1516, leaving a workshop that had trained the next generation of Venetian masters and a body of work that Berenson calls “the greatest” produced by any Venetian of the fifteenth century (Section II, line 444).

entities/giovanni-cabot.title: Giovanni Cabot (John Cabot)
entities/giovanni-cabot.content:
Giovanni Cabot (John Cabot)

Giovanni Cabot’s 1497 voyage from Venice to Newfoundland under the English flag. Gold line = outward voyage from Venice via Bristol to Cape Bonavista, where he made landfall on 24 June 1497. Red dashed line = return voyage. The star marks the landfall; the Grand Banks fishing grounds are shown off Newfoundland. Ship annotation notes the Mathew (50 tons, ~18 crew).
Giovanni Caboto (c. 1450–1500), known in English as John Cabot, was a Venetian navigator and explorer who, sailing for England, made the first European landfall on the North American mainland since the Norse voyages, discovering Newfoundland in 1497. He represents Venice’s brief but significant engagement with the Atlantic exploration that would ultimately eclipse the Mediterranean world.
Venetian Origins
Despite the Genoese-sounding name “Caboto,” Giovanni Cabot obtained Venetian citizenship after fifteen years of residence, around 1472. He married a Venetian woman, Mattea, and his son Sebastian was born in Venice (Lane, p. 277). As a merchant, he travelled widely in the Levant, visiting Mecca and gaining firsthand knowledge of the spice routes from the East.
Lane notes that Cabot was one of the “citizens-by-birth and those naturalized” who formed the mercantile backbone of Venetian commerce (Lane, p. 344). His career exemplifies the cosmopolitan, risk-taking spirit that drove Venetian merchants to the far corners of the known world.
The Columbus Inspiration
Cabot was in Valencia in 1493, working on a harbour-improvement project, when Christopher Columbus passed through on his triumphant return from the first voyage west. Cabot, who had read Marco Polo and spoken with Indian merchants in the Levant, doubted that Columbus had really reached Asia (Lane, pp. 277–278).
“He was well enough informed to know what Columbus had not done — to sail west to Cathay,” Lane writes (p. 278). Cabot believed the practical way to Asia was to cross the western sea in high latitudes — where the Earth was less wide — and then follow the coast south to the spice lands (Lane, p. 278).
The English Enterprise
Cabot took his project to England, where he interested King Henry VII, “who was alert for commercial opportunities” (Lane, p. 278). He also won support from Bristol merchants who already had experience crossing the western ocean. The seamen of western England had been trading and fishing off Iceland for more than a century and may have already discovered the Grand Banks, though they kept their knowledge quiet to avoid competition (Lane, p. 278).
In 1497, Cabot sailed from Bristol in a small ship called the Matthew — named after his Venetian wife — with a crew of only eighteen, including two Bristol merchants. After thirty-five days crossing the Atlantic, he made landfall on Newfoundland or perhaps Cape Breton (Lane, pp. 278–280).
Lane records that Cabot planted not only the banners of England and the pope, but also “the standard of Saint Mark” (Lane, p. 280), asserting the Venetian Republic’s symbolic presence in the new-found lands.
The Returns and Final Voyage
Cabot reported that he had found a large land mass, and his claims were taken seriously by the English king and the Bristol merchants. A new expedition of five ships sailed the following year, expecting to push on far enough to find the trade centres of Cathay. “But John Cabot and his ship never came back” (Lane, p. 280).
His achievements were later obscured by the exaggerations of his son Sebastian, who claimed credit for his father’s discoveries and who became the Spanish Pilot Major under Charles V (Lane, pp. 280–281). John Cabot’s English companions had been more experienced in northern waters, and while he was respected as a geographer and cosmographer, Lane notes he “seems to have enjoyed less acceptance as a practical expert in navigation” (Lane, p. 280).
Venetian Context
Cabot’s voyages belong to a period when Venice was acutely aware of the Portuguese and Spanish discoveries but was unable — or unwilling — to participate directly in Atlantic exploration. The Republic’s political structure, with its emphasis on the collective security of the Levant trade, made it difficult to gamble on the kind of state-sponsored expeditions that Portugal and Spain were pursuing (Lane, pp. 277, 298–300).
Cabot’s choice to seek English patronage reflected this Venetian limitation. Had the Republic been able to sponsor transatlantic discovery, the history of North America might have been different. As it was, Cabot remained a Venetian who sailed under an English flag — a symbol of the maritime republic’s reach and its limits.

entities/great-council.title: The Great Council
entities/great-council.content:
The Great Council
The Great Council (Maggior Consiglio) was the sovereign body of the Venetian Republic — the assembly of all adult male nobles from which all magistracies, councils, and committees derived their authority. It was the foundation on which the entire Venetian constitution rested. From the Serrata of 1297 until the Republic’s fall in 1797, membership in the Great Council was the defining mark of Venetian nobility.
Origins and the Serrata (1297)
Before the late 13th century, membership in the Great Council was fluid and somewhat haphazard. A majority of its members attended because of some office they held or had held — a judgeship, a seat in the Forty or the Senate. Each year a small nominating committee (as few as four men, chosen partially by lot) named one hundred additional members. Nomination was practically equivalent to election. This system worked reasonably well when Venice was small, but by the 13th century the population had grown markedly and competition for seats had become intense (Lane, pp. 132-133).
The reform of 1297 — the famous Serrata del Gran Consiglio (Closure of the Great Council) — was a masterstroke of aristocratic statecraft. It removed all limits on the Council’s size and provided that all those who had been members in the last four years would continue to be members thereafter, subject only to approval by twelve votes in the Council of Forty. At the same time, a nominating committee of three (proposed by the doge and his Council) could propose new members. The effect was to lock the existing ruling families into permanent, hereditary power (Lane, pp. 133-134).
The Serrata is often called the “closure” of the Council, but Lane observes that it made membership hereditary and life-long, giving all members of the ruling class assurance that they would not suddenly be excluded. The bitter animosities between families were submerged by the sheer number of families — nearly two hundred — sharing power. It became easier to find nobles who could act with impartiality (Lane, pp. 134-135).
Structure and Functions
The Great Council was Venice’s ultimate legislative and electoral body. It elected all magistrates, approved all laws, and had the final word on all major issues of war, peace, and finance. Its membership numbered about 1,500 adult noblemen in the 15th century, rising to over 2,000 by the 16th. The Council met in the Sala del Maggior Consiglio in the Ducal Palace — a vast hall measuring 54 by 25 meters, one of the largest rooms in Europe at the time, capable of seating more than fifteen hundred (Lane, p. 275).
The hall was decorated with one of the most ambitious painting cycles in Renaissance art. On the end wall hung Tintoretto’s Paradise (1588-1594), the largest oil painting on canvas in the world, depicting the celestial hierarchy of saints and blessed souls arrayed before Christ and the Virgin. Along the walls ran the cycle of Venetian history and myth, including Doge Enrico Dandolo’s conquest of Constantinople, the Peace of Venice (1177), and other legitimizing narratives.
Elections and Procedures
Balloting in the Great Council was a complex affair designed to prevent fraud, intimidation, and faction-building. Multiple rounds of voting — using a combination of lot and ballot — were used to select nominating committees, who then proposed candidates for the full Council to approve. Ballot boxes (called ballottini or sacchetti) were carried through the aisles by designated collectors. The Three Chiefs of the Council of Ten sat in positions of prominence to oversee the enforcement of election rules, ensuring that no noble could manipulate the system (Lane, p. 275).
Social Meaning
The Great Council’s membership defined the Venetian nobility (nobili). Those enrolled in the Libro d’Oro (Golden Book) formed a hereditary caste distinct from the cittadini (citizens) and the popolani (common people). Within the Council, all nobles were theoretically equal; no titles of marquis, count, or baron were recognized among Venetians. This egalitarianism within the ruling class was a source of great pride and a key to the Republic’s internal stability.
Yet the Council was too large for detailed deliberation. That function passed to smaller bodies: the Senate, the Council of Ten, and the Collegio. The Great Council remained supreme in name, but its real power lay in its electoral function — the right to choose who would fill those smaller, more powerful councils and magistracies.
Decline and Fall
The Great Council met for the last time on May 12, 1797, when Napoleon Bonaparte demanded the dissolution of the Venetian Republic. Under the threat of French bayonets, the Council voted itself out of existence, ending more than five centuries of aristocratic rule. Napoleon subsequently ceded Venice to Austria by the Treaty of Campo Formio (October 1797).

entities/leonardo-loredan.title: Leonardo Loredan
entities/leonardo-loredan.content:
Leonardo Loredan
Leonardo Loredan (1436–1521) was Doge of Venice from 1501 to 1521, presiding over the Republic during the darkest days of the League of Cambrai crisis. He is famous for the serene and dignified portrait by Giovanni Bellini (Figure 24 in Lane), which has become one of the most recognisable images of Venetian leadership — and for presiding over the cataclysm of Agnadello and the slow, painful recovery that followed.
The Loredan Family and Venetian History
The Loredan were one of the great “apostolic families” — case apostoliche — of Venice, claiming descent from the earliest settlement of the lagoon. The family had produced doges (Leonardo Loredan was not the first), admirals, and senators across several centuries. A Loredan had won the decisive naval battle at Gallipoli in 1416 that temporarily broke Ottoman sea power in the Aegean; Pietro Loredan had led Venetian forces against the Turks in the 1440s. The family’s identity was intertwined with Venice’s maritime and military history.
Most pointedly for the politics of Loredan’s election, it was “a Loredan” who had led the Council of Ten that deposed the aged Doge Francesco Foscari in 1457 — the last act of a family feud that had festered for decades between the Loredan and Foscari clans (Lane, p. 14112). When Leonardo Loredan was elected doge in 1501, he represented a family that had been at the apex of Venetian power for a generation.
Election and Character
Loredan was elected doge in 1501, “popular at the moment because a French alliance he had favoured was proving successful and because a member of his family had just died a hero’s death in the Turkish war” (Lane, p. 269). He was described as soave (suave) and sbarbato (smooth-shaven) — a contrast to the bearded, more imperious doges of the earlier fifteenth century. Lane characterises him as “a smooth chairman and an effective orator” (Lane, p. 14129). His portrait by Giovanni Bellini — the great diptych in the National Gallery, London — shows the doge in his ceremonial corno (ducal horn, the distinctive peaked cap of Venetian doges) and richly embroidered dogalina (ducal robe). The face is calm, almost impassive: the eyes carry a suggestion of the burdens of office, but no anxiety. It is the portrait of a man accustomed to power.
Formation of the League of Cambrai
The League of Cambrai (1508) was the most dangerous diplomatic combination Venice had ever faced. Pope Julius II, Emperor Maximilian I, King Louis XII of France, and King Ferdinand of Aragon — joined eventually by most of the other Italian states — formed a coalition aimed at dismembering the Venetian terraferma empire. The immediate cause was Venetian expansion on the Italian mainland, which had alarmed every neighbouring power; the deeper cause was the widespread resentment of Venetian wealth and commercial privilege.
Venice had been warned. Hazlitt records that Henry VIII of England was initially friendly toward Venice and made diplomatic efforts at the Vatican on the Republic’s behalf, attempting to soften the Pope’s hostility. But these efforts came to nothing against Julius II’s determination to recover Papal territories that Venice controlled.
The Disaster of Agnadello (May 14, 1509)
The French army under Marshal Trivulzio met the Venetian forces at Agnadello (Ghiara d’Adda) on 14 May 1509. The Venetian army, led by the condottiero Niccolò di Pitigliano (Pitigliano), was shattered. Pitigliano “failed to support” the troops that engaged the French, the battle cry “Italia e San Marco!” rang out as the army broke, and within weeks, city after city on the mainland — Vicenza, Verona, Brescia, even Padua — fell or surrendered (Lane, pp. 12838–12852).
When news reached Venice, Loredan was famously depicted by Marin Sanudo in his Diarii as “acting half-dead at receipt of the bad news” (Lane, p. 270). Sanudo contrasted this despondency with the spirited behaviour of Doge Francesco Foscari, who after earlier defeats had appeared before the councils “confidently dressed in his most gorgeous golden robes.” The contrast was unflattering to Loredan and has coloured all subsequent assessments of his dogeship.
Recovery: The Tax Debate
Despite his initial paralysis, Loredan roused himself to exert the constitutional leadership expected of him. In the summer of 1509, a severe measure to force payment of heavy war taxes on real estate was voted down in the Great Council — 700 noes to 650 ayes — a stunning demonstration of patrician reluctance to fund a war they associated with their own oligarchic losses. “Doge Loredan took the rostrum to plead eloquently for the needs of the emergency and swung the Great Council around so that it passed an amended version, 864 to 494 noes” (Lane, p. 14179). This turnaround — from 700 against to 494 against on the same day — was a real political achievement that Lane credits to Loredan’s oratorical skill.
The money financed the extraordinary military operation led by Andrea Gritti: between 120,000 and 200,000 ducats were minted from melted-down jewellery and silverware to pay the emergency troops. The Council of Ten, operating in crisis mode, authorised expenditures and extraordinary measures that in normal times would have been unthinkable.
Recapture of Padua and the War’s Course
The effective military leadership during the crisis came not from Loredan but from Andrea Gritti, who recaptured Padua in July 1509 with a night assault and then organised its defence against Emperor Maximilian’s siege army, which brought “the most formidable artillery yet used in any siege” (Lane, p. 245). Loredan’s role was the constitutional one: maintaining the unity of the patriciate, managing the Great Council, and providing the political and financial framework for Gritti’s operations.
This division of labour — the doge as constitutional chairman, the military hero as field commander — reflected the Venetian system at its most functional. Loredan was never a military figure; he was a politician and administrator. His value lay precisely in his ability to hold the Great Council together through years of financial pressure, diplomatic humiliation, and military setback.
Later Years and the Recovery of Position
The Treaty of Blois (1513) and subsequent diplomatic settlements gradually restored Venice’s position. By the time of Loredan’s death in 1521, Venice had survived the League of Cambrai — not unscathed, but intact. It had lost some mainland territories temporarily, paid reparations, and made painful concessions, but it had retained the core of its state, its independence, and its commercial empire. The Republic’s recovery owed much to its ability to play off its enemies against each other and to the basic resilience of its financial and administrative system.
Hazlitt records the splendour of Loredan’s funeral ceremonies, which confirmed his status as a doge who had guided the Republic through its darkest hour with at least formal dignity.
He was succeeded by the octogenarian Antonio Grimani (r. 1521–1523), whose brief dogeship gave way to Andrea Gritti (1523–1538) — the man who had done the most to save the Republic that Loredan had notionally governed.
The Bellini Portrait as Historical Document
Loredan’s lasting fame rests heavily on Giovanni Bellini’s portrait, painted around 1501 — the year of his election — and now hanging in the National Gallery, London. The portrait is remarkable for its psychological depth and technical mastery: the doge’s face is modelled in thin glazes that give the skin an almost luminous quality, the corno is rendered with the delicacy of embroidery, and the elaborate gold and white dogalina displays Bellini’s mastery of textile depiction. It remains one of the most psychologically acute portraits of the Renaissance.
