A classic critical essay on Venetian Renaissance painting by one of the most influential art historians of the late 19th century. Berenson argues that Venetian painting is “the most complete expression in art of the Italian Renaissance.” The work combines an interpretive essay with exhaustive indices of works by major Venetian masters, organized by location. Berenson based his attributions on first-hand examination of the paintings.
The third edition includes expanded coverage of provincial galleries and private collections in Britain, France, and Germany, and adds Beccaruzzi, Caprioli, Polidoro, Lanzani, Rocco Marconi, Andrea Schiavone, and Girolamo da Treviso to the lists.
Contents
Note to the Third Edition — revisions to gallery numbering, additions to painter lists, new provenance information.
Note to the Second Edition — revisions to indices.
Preface (pp. vii–xii) — Berenson’s thesis on Venetian painting as the fullest expression of the Renaissance spirit. Discussion of Crivelli, the critical method of Morelli and others, and the role of photography in connoisseurship.
The Venetian Painters of the Renaissance (pp. 1–75):







































































































































SectionTitlePageIValue of Venetian Art1IIThe Church and Painting2IIIThe Renaissance5IVPainting and the Renaissance12VPageant Pictures17VIPainting and the Confraternities22VIIEasel Pictures and Giorgione26VIIIThe Giorgionesque Spirit31IXThe Portrait32XThe Young Titian38XIApparent Failure of the Renaissance41XIILotto43XIIIThe Late Renaissance and Titian44XIVHumanity and the Renaissance48XVSebastiano del Piombo49XVITintoretto51XVIIValue of Minor Episodes in Art56XVIIITintoretto’s Portraits59XIXVenetian Art and the Provinces60XXPaul Veronese62XXIBassano, Genre, and Landscape64XXIIThe Venetians and Velasquez70XXIIIDecline of Venetian Art71XXIVLonghi72XXVCanaletto and Guardi74
Index to the Works of the Principal Venetian Painters — detailed catalog of paintings by each major Venetian master, organized by location (galleries, churches, private collections in and out of Italy).
Index of Places — cross-reference by city and institution.
Relevance to Venice Wiki
Essential source for the Florentine and Venetian art worlds of the 15th–16th centuries. Berenson covers the major painters active in Venice during the period: the Bellini family, Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto, Veronese, Lotto, Carpaccio, Palma Vecchio, Lorenzo Lotto, and many others. The indices provide a comprehensive survey of what existed in Venetian churches, scuole, and collections. The essay itself is a classic statement on Venetian Renaissance aesthetics.

sources/bianchi-giovini-biografia-fra-pa.title: Bianchi-Giovini — Biografia di fra Paolo Sarpi
sources/bianchi-giovini-biografia-fra-pa.content:
Biografia di fra Paolo Sarpi, teologo e consultore di stato della Repubblica Veneta
Aurelio Angelo Bianchi-Giovini, Biografia di fra Paolo Sarpi, teologo e consultore di stato della Repubblica Veneta (second original edition, Turin: Poligrafia Italiana, 1850). Biography in Italian. Raw text: 28,416 lines (830 scanned pages; University of Minnesota copy).
A full-length biography of the Servite friar Paolo Sarpi (1552–1623) — the theologian and state consultant who defended the Venetian Republic against the papacy during the Interdict of 1606–1607 and wrote the celebrated History of the Council of Trent. Bianchi-Giovini (1799–1862), an anti-clerical historian, presents Sarpi as a scientist, reformer of abuses, and champion of state authority against the Roman Curia. This is his own corrected second original edition; in his preface he recounts the pirated editions and errors of earlier printings, and the work was issued in two volumes printed in different places amid the political disturbances of 1848–1850.
Contents
The biography follows Sarpi’s life in thirty chapters (Capi). It opens with an assessment of the man and his fame — a friar whose name divided the two great religious factions of his age, celebrated by one and hated by the other.
Capo I–IV cover Sarpi’s origins, birth and early life, his entry into the Order of the Servi, his formation and early studies. Bianchi-Giovini emphasises that Sarpi was by nature destined for the physical and mathematical sciences, and was drawn only by unforeseen events onto the turbulent political scene.
Capo V–X treat his rise as a scholar and theologian — his mathematical and scientific learning, his distance from the visionary doctrines of the alchemists, his scientific correspondence, and the early reputation that made him consultore. The biography traces the state of the Church and the papacy in his day, the strength of the Roman Curia, and Sarpi’s growing position within Venetian intellectual life.
Capo XI–XVIII move to the great church–state controversies that made him famous. The narrative covers the Venetian disputes with Rome, Sarpi’s appointment as consultore di stato (“state consultant”), his part in the controversies over the clergy, ecclesiastical property, the Inquisition in Venice, the prohibition of books, and the resistance of the Republic to papal jurisdiction — the ground of his later reputation.
Capo XIX–XXVIII include the central events of his public career: the Interdict of 1606–1607, when Venice, with Sarpi as its spokesman, defied the interdict laid by Pope Paul V and the Jesuits’ expulsion from Venetian territory; the conspiracy of the mercenaries against Venice (1618) revealed to the Doge and punished by the Council of Ten; the writing and publication at London (1619) of his Istoria del Concilio Tridentino (History of the Council of Trent), surreptitiously carried abroad by Marc’Antonio de Dominis, and the controversy it provoked with the papal historian Sforza Pallavicino; his works on ecclesiastical benefices, the church’s wealth, and the Uscocchi of the Adriatic; his astronomical observations and his share in the invention of the telescope; and his friendship with and prophecies concerning Galileo.
Capo XXIX–XXX close with Sarpi’s later years — his solitary life, his reception of the Dutch ambassador Aersens, the tragedy of Antonio Foscarini, the attempts of Rome (under Paul V, Gregory XV and Urban VIII) to have him removed, his final illness and death in 1623, his funeral, the opposition of Urban VIII to a monument for him, and the fate of his tomb. The biography ends with notices of Fra Fulgenzio, his companion, and observations on his skull.
The volume concludes with an Appendice bibliografica in several sections: Sarpi’s published works and editions; his unedited works divided into Consult (opinions), the Bergantini collection, and other papers; the works he edited; those falsely attributed to him; a project for a new Sarpian edition; and a list of his biographers, with his epitaph.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome X
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome X (Livre XL)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome X. Survey history in French. Raw text: 11,489 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome X contains Livre XL, the concluding and thematic volume of Daru’s history — “Of the sciences, of literature and of the arts among the Venetians” — a reflective survey of the intellectual and artistic achievement of the Republic as a whole, closing the work.
Contents
Livre XL — Of the sciences, literature and arts of the Venetians. Daru turns from the political, military, industrial and commercial record to estimate what the Venetian people contributed to European knowledge and civilisation. He reflects that, after fourteen centuries of existence, some discoveries in the sciences and some monuments of the arts are all that remains of this celebrated people. He weighs how the mercantile spirit spread throughout the nation, and the silent obedience demanded by a suspicious government, were unfavourable to the development of thought, but how the opulence procured by commerce, the voyages and the internal peace balanced those causes. The Livre surveys Venetian achievement across the sciences, letters and the fine arts.
The volume then presents a long appendix, the Notice des manuscrits et pièces justificatives — a descriptive catalogue of the manuscripts and documentary pieces (in Italian and French) on which the history draws, including such items as a description of the arsenal of Venice (1613), accounts of the Venetian navy and galleys, and ordinances of the Senate, followed by Fin du Tome Dixième.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome XI (Notice des manuscrits)
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome XI (Notice des manuscrits)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome XI. Reference volume in French. Raw text: 13,624 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome XI is the Notice des manuscrits et pièces justificatives — Daru’s descriptive catalogue of the manuscript and documentary sources on which his history is built. It contains no continuous narrative; it is the scholarly apparatus that documents the archive and library materials behind the whole work. It is thus relevant as the evidentiary companion to the narrative Tomes I–X, useful for tracing where Daru’s account of any period or topic draws its material.
Contents
The volume is organised by sections classifying the sources by type:

Section III — Histoire générale et pièces historiques (General history and historical pieces), beginning with Antiquités (Antiquities) — the earliest writers on the Venetian people, such as the Memorie antiche de’ popoli Veneti of Alessandro Zilioli, the Historia Euganea of Anselm, and the anonymous early chronicler of the Venetians (a codex of about 1210), with notes on the libraries (Venice, the Vatican, Treviso) that held them.
Section IV — Histoires spéciales (Special histories), opening with the particular histories of cities and provinces (Asolo, and other localities), followed by other categories of special histories.
Section V — Correspondance et rapports des ambassadeurs (Correspondence and reports of the ambassadors), beginning with the correspondence of the French ambassadors to Venice, for which Daru notes the difficulty of research of this kind.

The volume closes with Fin du Tome Onzième. The detailed index to this Notice is provided in Tome XII.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome XII (Tables)
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome XII (Liste des Doges et Tables)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome XII. Reference volume in French. Raw text: 16,706 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome XII is the closing reference volume of the work — the Liste des Doges and the general tables and index. It contains no continuous narrative; it is the finding aid to the whole Histoire de la République de Venise (Tomes I–X) and its apparatus (Tome XI). It is relevant as the key for navigating the full set.
Contents
The volume opens with the Liste des Doges — the complete list of the doges of the Republic, beginning with the magistrats antérieurs aux doges (the consuls sent by Padua to govern the port of Rialto, about the year 400), through Albert Faliero, Thomas Candiano, Conon Daulo, Marin Linio, and the whole succession of Venetian doges down to the end of the Republic, ending with Fin de la Liste des doges.
The volume then contains the general tables:

Table des matières des pièces justificatives — the contents table of the documentary pièces justificatives.
Table de la notice des manuscrits — the contents table of the Notice des manuscrits of Tome XI.
Table alphabétique des matières — the alphabetical general index of the whole work, running through the entire alphabet, with entries such as the state of the Republic’s revenues at the beginning of the fifteenth century, the Venetian lira and its weight, and countless other topics and names cross-referenced to the relevant tomes and pages.

The volume ends with Fin., closing the complete edition.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome III
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome III (Livres XIII–XVI)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome III. Survey history in French. Raw text: 11,180 lines. This is the Wouters 1840 edition, continuing the Gutenberg e-volumes of Tomes I–II.
Tome III covers Livres XIII–XVI, the Venetian wars of conquest on the Italian mainland in the 1420s–1440s, fought chiefly against the dukes of Milan. It is the volume that carries Venice to the height of its terraferma empire in the generation before the League of Cambrai.
Contents
Livre XIII opens with the deliberation on the war proposed by the Florentines against the Duke of Milan. It covers the death of Doge Tommaso Mocenigo (1420–1423), the acquisition and loss of Salonika, the declaration of war against the Duke of Milan, the siege of Brescia, and the victories of Francesco Carmagnola — the peace by which the Republic acquired Brescia (1423–1426).
Livre XIV continues the war against the Duke of Milan with the battle of Macalo won by Carmagnola, the acquisition of Bergamo (1426–1428), the peace of 1428, the Republic’s acquisition of the expectancy of the principality of Ravenna, the third war against the Duke of Milan, and the death of Carmagnola (1428–1433).
Livre XV covers the fourth war against the Duke of Milan — the campaigns of Piccinino and Gatta-Melata, the siege of Brescia, the appearance of Francesco Sforza on the theatre of war, the taking and retaking of Verona, and the peace of 1441 by which the Republic acquired Lonato, Valeggio and Peschiera and usurped the state of Ravenna (1433–1441).
Livre XVI treats the war in the Milanese, the death of Filippo Maria Visconti, the war of the Venetians against the Milanese and against Francesco Sforza, and the peace that confirmed the Republic’s conquests in Lombardy.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome IV
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome IV (Livres XVII–XXI)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome IV. Survey history in French. Raw text: 12,245 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome IV covers Livres XVII–XXI, the wars of the later fifteenth century in the Levant and in Italy: the Venetian struggles against the Turks (the loss of Negroponte), the acquisition of Cyprus, the defence of the Morea, and the French expedition of Charles VIII into Italy that first shattered the Italian balance of power.
Contents
Livre XVII opens with the treaty of commerce with the Sultan of Egypt and the war against the Turks in the Morea. It covers the project of crusade, the loss of the island of Negroponte, the alliance with Persia, the war in Asia Minor and Albania, the defence of Scutari, the peace with the Sultan and the loss of Scutari (1457–1479), and the affairs of Cyprus — the Republic’s acquisition of that kingdom and the union of Vegia and Zante to the dominion.
Livre XVIII treats the war of the Florentines allied with the Venetians against the Pope and the King of Naples, the league of the Republic with the Pope, and the calling of the Turks into the kingdom of Naples.
Livre XIX is a celebrated tableau of the commerce of the Venetians — their manufactures and their marine — written, as Daru notes, at the moment when Venice was about to lose the empire of commerce it had exercised for four or five centuries.
Livre XX covers the expedition of Charles VIII to Naples (1494–1498) — the descent of the French into Italy, the alarm of the Italian states, and the beginnings of the foreign intervention that would dominate the next decades.
Livre XXI treats the war against the Turks and the conquest of the island of Cephalonia, the alliance of the Republic with Louis XII of France and its acquisition of the Cremonese, the expulsion of Ludovico Sforza from the throne of Milan (1499–1501), the French expedition to Naples under Louis XII with the conquest, partition and loss of that kingdom, and the efforts of Cardinal d’Amboise.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome V
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome V (Livres XXII–XXVIII)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome V. Survey history in French. Raw text: 11,403 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome V covers Livres XXII–XXVIII, the central decades of the sixteenth century — the disaster of the League of Cambrai and the battle of Agnadel (1509), the wars that followed for the recovery of the terraferma, the long peace with the Turks, and the culminating War of Cyprus and the battle of Lepanto (1570–1573).
Contents
Livre XXII opens with the Ligue de Cambrai (1509) — the coalition formed against Venice — and the battle of Agnadel, in which the Republic lost all its mainland provinces at a stroke. It is the great turning-point of Venetian power in Italy.
Livre XXIII covers the campaign of 1510, the Diet of the Empire, the harangue of Hélian, the league of the Pope, the Venetians, the Swiss and the King of Aragon against Louis XII, the fruitless attempts on Verona and Genoa, the Council of Tours, and the Pope’s entry into Bologna and the siege of Mirandola.
Livre XXIV covers the campaign of 1513 and the division of the confederates against Venice.
Livre XXV continues the wars of recovery of the Venetian mainland in the 1510s–1520s.
Livre XXVI treats the vacancy of the throne of Milan and the war against the Turks (1530–1540), the acquisition of Marano in the Friuli, and the peace of thirty years (1540–1570) — the period in which Europe’s attention turned to the progress of Luther’s Reformation and the growing power of the Ottoman empire.
Livre XXVII is the War of Cyprus — the sieges of Nicosia and Famagusta (1570–1573) — and the battle of Lepanto, in which the Republic, after sixty-five years of maintaining itself, fought alongside the Christian league.
Livre XXVIII covers the peace of thirty years, the passage of Henry III of France through Venice, the plague of 1575, the recognition of Henry IV as king of France by the Venetians, the acquisition of Ferrara by the Holy See (1574–1604), and a survey of the situation of the Venetian government at that epoch.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome VI
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome VI (Livres XXIX–XXXI)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome VI. Survey history in French. Raw text: 11,705 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome VI covers Livres XXIX–XXXI, the great church–state crisis of the early seventeenth century and the wars that followed. It opens with the Interdict of Paul V (1605–1607), the confrontation in which Venice, with Fra Paolo Sarpi as its spokesman, defied papal authority — the period of the Uscocchi war and the War of Montferrat, and the conspiracy of 1618.
Contents
Livre XXIX opens with the dispute between the Republic and Pope Paul V (1605–1607). Daru recounts how the Republic, which had long held its clergy in obedience and repelled the pretensions of the popes, found a new occasion to proclaim its maxims; the narrative centres on the interdict laid on Venice, the resistance of the Senate, the role of the theologian Fra Paolo Sarpi and the Servite friars, and the eventual accommodation.
Livre XXX covers the war of the Uscocchi and the war of Montferrat (1607–1618). It opens with the consolidation of the Republic’s external peace after the settlement with the Holy See, and its loss of the powerful ally Henry IV of France (assassinated 1610). The narrative covers the depredations of the Uscocchi pirates of the Adriatic, the ensuing conflict with the House of Austria, and the war in Italy over the Montferrat succession.
Livre XXXI treats the conspiracy of 1618 — the plot, connected with Spain and the archduke Ferdinand, against the Venetian state — its discovery, and the stern punishment meted out by the Republic, including the execution of the French ambassador’s secretary Antonio Foscarini, a subject Daru treats at length.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome VII
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome VII (Livres XXXII–XXXV)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome VII. Survey history in French. Raw text: 9,362 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome VII covers Livres XXXII–XXXV, the long seventeenth-century decline and the last great eastern war: the Valtelline and Mantuan wars, the twenty-five-year War of Candia (1644–1669) against the Turks, the brief recovery of the Morea under Morosini and the peace of Carlowitz, and the eighteenth-century neutrals into the middle of the century.
Contents
Livre XXXII covers the war of the Valtelline and the war for the succession of Mantua, together with the changes in the attributions of the Council of Ten, the démêlés with the Pope, and the quarrels with the Turks in the period 1618–1644.
Livre XXXIII is the War of Candia (1644–1669) — the long and exhausting struggle for the island of Crete against the Ottoman empire, which Daru opens by reflecting on why the Turks, harbouring a deep resentment against the Republic, had so readily granted it peace and yet found so good an occasion to satisfy their enmity.
Livre XXXIV covers the conquest of the Morea by the Venetians under Francesco Morosini, and the peace of Carlowitz (1699), followed by the neutrality of the Venetians in the years 1700–1713 during the War of the Spanish Succession.
Livre XXXV treats the war for the succession of Parma and Tuscany, the neutrality of the Venetians in that war and in the later war for the succession of the Emperor Charles VI, the division of the patriarchate of Aquileia (1719–1750), the wars of Europe in the second half of the eighteenth century, and the wars of the Republic with the various powers.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome VIII
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome VIII (Livres XXXVI–XXXVII)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome VIII. Survey history in French. Raw text: 9,067 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome VIII covers Livres XXXVI–XXXVII, the last phase of the Republic: the decay of the Venetian navy and fortifications, the impact of the French Revolution, and the onset of the crisis with the campaigns of General Bonaparte in Italy (1796–1797) that ended in the preliminaries of Léoben — the events immediately preceding the fall of Venice.
Contents
Livre XXXVI examines the state of the Republic on the eve of its ruin. Daru surveys the failure of Venetian naval construction to keep pace with other nations, the fortifications of the places falling into ruin — fortresses he calls emblems of the Republic’s history, their giant dimensions recalling the age of its opulence and pride.
Livre XXXVII opens with the campaigns of General Bonaparte in Italy, the revolution at Bergamo and Brescia, the insurrection of the populace of the Venetian provinces against the French, the signing of the preliminaries of peace at Léoben, and the massacre of Verona (the “Veronese Easter”). These events set the stage for the Republic’s dissolution, which Tome IX takes up directly.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome IX
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome IX (Livres XXXVIII–XXXIX)
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Brussels: Grégoire Wouters, 1840), Tome IX. Survey history in French. Raw text: 9,596 lines. The Wouters 1840 edition.
Tome IX covers Livres XXXVIII–XXXIX, the climax of the work — the negotiations of the Treaty of Campo Formio and the dissolution of the Republic of Venice (May 1797–January 1798) — together with Daru’s celebrated analysis of the Venetian constitution and government.
Contents
Livre XXXVIII is the story of the fall itself. Daru recounts the negotiations of the treaty of Campo Formio, and how the Venetians, about to have to struggle alone against the whole French army, were not yet initiated into the mystery of what had been agreed at Léoben. He describes the confusion that spread through the chamber when the news broke — the nobility believing itself on the point of being massacred, the members of the council rising from their places crying Aux voix! aux voix!, and the resolution dissolving the Republic sanctioned by five hundred and twelve votes against a dozen. He narrates the abdication of the Great Council and the ending of the thousand-year-old state.
Livre XXXIX is Daru’s Description of the government of Venice. He writes that the study of history would satisfy only curiosity if, after the recital of facts, one did not stop to observe their consequences. He analyses the result of the Republic’s first eight centuries — a form of government highly complicated and highly vaunted — tracing the constitution, the magistracies, the Council of Ten, the Inquisitors of State, and the character of Venetian rule as it developed and as it declined.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome Premier
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome Premier
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Paris, 1819), Tome Premier. Survey history in French. Raw text: 6,036 lines (Project Gutenberg e-text 46631). Daru (1767–1829), a French soldier, administrator and academician, wrote his monumental seven-volume history of Venice from the archives while serving as Intendant during the French occupation.
This Gutenberg edition is bound in two e-volumes; the present Tome Premier covers Livres I–VIII, from the origins of Venice through the early fourteenth century (to the election of Marin Giorgi, 1310). It is the first half of a work that in Daru’s full edition extends to the fall of the Republic in 1797. Note: this e-volume stops at 1310 — the sixteenth-century and later coverage promised by the folder is NOT in this edition; see the gap note on the folder.
Contents
Livre I opens with a geographical description and the origin of the Venetians — the state of the Veneti under the Romans, and the invasions of the Goths, Huns and Lombards that drove them into the lagoons. Daru reflects on the singular origin, position and fortune of a republic that left no model behind it.
Livre II (after the interregnum of the correcteurs des lois) covers the internal divisions of the early dogate — the enterprise of Jean Participatio against the county of Comacchio, the Venetian fleet beaten by the Saracens, the rivalry with Obelerio and the burning of Malamocco (830), the conjuration against the doge, the rise of Carossio, and the dogate of Pierre Tradenigo (836) with the troubles of the factions.
Livre III covers the reign of Sébastien Ziani and the outrages done to the Venetians by the Greek emperor — the blinding of the ambassador (Henri Dandolo) by Manuel, the démêlés between Pope Alexander III and the emperor, and the institution of the forced loans (emprunts forcés) that became habitual and were levied at a hundredth of each citizen’s fortune.
Livre IV is the reign of Henri Dandolo (1192): the war against the Pisans, the Fourth Crusade (1199), the taking of Zara, the excommunication of the Venetians, and the conquest of Constantinople (1202–1204) that made Venice mistress of an eastern empire of naval bases.
Livre V covers the dogate of Pierre Ziani (1205), the occupation of Corfu and Candia, the wars against the Genoese, the revolts of Candia (1205–1228), and the dogates that followed.
Livre VI treats the election of Pierre Gradenigo, the disasters in the East and the war against the Genoese (1289–1299), together with Daru’s extended considerations on the nature of governments and the gradual narrowing of the popular role in the election of the prince.
Livre VII recounts the conjuration of Marin Bocconio, the affairs of Ferrara, the Republic’s usurpation of that city, and the excommunication of the Venetians (c. 1300), with the resentment of the nobles at the usurpation of power.
Livre VIII covers the lifting of the interdict, the expedition against the Genoese, the revolt of Candia, the war against the lord of Verona, and the acquisition of further dominions. It closes with the election of Marin Giorgi as doge (1310), where the Tome Premier ends.
The volume’s body text closes at the election of Marin Giorgi (1310), followed by the Table des matières for Tome Premier.

sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.title: Daru — Histoire de la République de Venise, Tome Second
sources/daru-histoire-republique-venise-.content:
Histoire de la République de Venise — Tome Second
Comte Pierre-Antoine-Noël-Bruno Daru, Histoire de la République de Venise (Paris, 1819), Tome Second. Survey history in French. Raw text: 20,424 lines (Project Gutenberg e-text 46632). The second of the two Gutenberg e-volumes of Daru’s great history.
This Tome Second covers Livres IX–XVII, the wars and conquests of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, from the war against the King of Hungary (1355) through the acquisition of Zante and Cephalonia (1483). Note: this e-volume ends at 1483 — Daru’s full edition continues to the fall of the Republic in 1797, but the sixteenth-century and later coverage is NOT in this set; see the gap note on the folder.
Contents
Livre IX covers the war against the King of Hungary and the loss of Dalmatia, a fresh plague at Venice (1355–1361), the foundation of the Library of Saint Mark by Petrarch, the last revolts of Candia, the expedition against Alexandria, the election of André Contarini (1361–1367), a new revolt of Trieste, the démêlé with the Bishop of Venice, and the war against the lord of Padua, the King of Hungary and the Duke of Austria.
Livre X is the War of Chioggia (1378–1381) — the league formed against Venice, the Republic without population or territory disputing its existence against a multitude of enemies, and the industry by which it created the means of resistance.
Livre XI recounts the war against Carrare, lord of Padua; the recovery of the Trévisan; the acquisition of Corfu, Durazzo, Alessio, Argos, Naples of Romania and Scutari (1382–1390); the league against the Turks, the battle of Nicopolis; Tamerlane’s defeat of Bajazet at Angora; a new rupture between the Genoese and Venetians (1388–1403); and the war in Lombardy against François Carrare.
Livre XII covers the acquisition of Zara and other Dalmatian places, of Lepanto and Patras; the treaty with the Turks; acquisitions on the Po; war with the King of Hungary and the truce (1406–1413); the refusal of Ancona; a momentary rupture with the Turks; the acquisition of Corinth; the death of Charles Zéno; and the war against the King of Hungary and the patriarch.
Livre XIII treats the deliberation on the war proposed by the Florentines against the Duke of Milan, the death of Doge Tommaso Mocenigo (1420–1423), the acquisition and loss of Salonika, the declaration of war against the Duke of Milan, the siege of Brescia, the victories of Francesco Carmagnola, and the peace by which the Republic acquired Brescia (1423–1426).
Livre XIV continues the war against the Duke of Milan, the battle of Macalo won by Carmagnola, the peace of 1428 and the acquisition of Bergamo, the Republic’s acquisition of the expectancy of the principality of Ravenna, the third war against the Duke of Milan with the Venetian defeat, and the death of Carmagnola (1428–1433).
Livre XV covers the fourth war against the Duke of Milan — the campaigns of Piccinino and Gatta-Melata, the siege of Brescia, the appearance of Francesco Sforza, the taking and retaking of Verona, and the peace of 1441 by which the Republic acquired Lonato, Valeggio and Peschiera and usurped the state of Ravenna (1433–1441).
Livre XVI treats the war in the Milanese, the death of Filippo Maria Visconti, the war of the Venetians against the Milanese and Francesco Sforza, the peace acquiring the province of Crema, the renewal of the war against Sforza and his coronation as Duke of Milan (1441–1450), the war against Sforza with the French as his auxiliaries, and the general pacification and league of Italy.
Livre XVII covers the treaty of commerce with the Sultan of Egypt, the war against the Turks in the Morea, the project of crusade, the loss of the island of Negroponte, the alliance with Persia, war in Asia Minor and Albania, the defence of Scutari, the peace with the Sultan and the loss of Scutari (1457–1479), the affairs of Cyprus and the Republic’s acquisition of that kingdom, and the union of the islands of Vegia and Zante to the dominion (to 1483).
The volume’s body text closes with the acquisition of Zante and Cephalonia (1483) and the words Fin du Tome Deuxième, followed by the volume’s Table des matières and the Project Gutenberg license.

sources/gratarol-narrazione-apologetica-.title: Gratarol — Narrazione Apologetica, Parte Prima
sources/gratarol-narrazione-apologetica-.content:
Narrazione Apologetica di Pier-Antonio Gratarol — Parte Prima
Pier-Antonio Gratarol, Narrazione Apologetica (third edition, Venice, MDCCXCVII — “Anno I della Libertà”), Parte Prima. First-person memoir and defence in Italian. Raw text: 8,941 lines (Columbia University Library copy).
One of the celebrated literary scandals of eighteenth-century Venice. Gratarol (1738–1785), a Venetian nobleman and Secretary of the Senate recently appointed Resident to the royal court of Naples, believed himself to have been made the laughing-stock of a comedy written by Count Carlo Gozzi. His Narrazione apologetica is his vindication, written in exile, explaining the affront, his flight from Venice and the injustice he claimed to have suffered. This is the third edition — reissued at Venice in 1797, the year the Republic fell, and in this case the two parts were published together with a preface and an appended set of letters.
Contents
The volume opens with an editor’s notice (Avviso) explaining how this edition came to be printed and the extraordinary fortune of the work, and then presents a letter from Gratarol that stands before the whole.
The body of Parte Prima is Gratarol’s narrative of the affair. He recounts how, on the point of departing for his post as Resident to the court of Naples, he discovered that Count Carlo Gozzi — a former Jesuit, here described as a man of sixty — had composed a comedy called Le Droghe d’Amore (The Love Potions), ostensibly taken from the Spanish, in which, Gratarol maintains, a character had been inserted solely to make sport and mockery of his person. He traces the origin of the affair to Gozzi’s partiality for a certain actress, narrates the intrigues that kept him ignorant of the comedy’s intent, and explains how a false supposition that he had taken part in some manoeuvre fed the quarrel.
Gratarol then sets out the consequences: the affront to his honour as an office-holder of the Senate, the actions of his enemies among the nobles, the public ridicule, and the pressure that left him little choice but to withdraw from Venice. He insists throughout on his innocence and on the reality of the conspiracy of ridicule mounted against him, appealing to the judgement of his fellow citizens and to posterity.
The Parte Prima carries the narrative from the first discovery of the comedy through the circumstances that drove him toward exile, closing as he resolves upon the step that Parte Seconda takes up — his departure from Venice.
The raw text’s quality is moderate: the 1797 Venice printing is scanned from a Columbia copy with some page-fragmentation, but the narrative is continuous and legible.

sources/gratarol-narrazione-apologetica-.title: Gratarol — Narrazione Apologetica, Parte Seconda
sources/gratarol-narrazione-apologetica-.content:
Narrazione Apologetica di Pier-Antonio Gratarol — Parte Seconda
Pier-Antonio Gratarol, Narrazione Apologetica (third edition, Venice, MDCCXCVII), Parte Seconda, “con l’Aggiunta delle Riflessioni d’un Imparziale precedute da una Lettera del medesimo Signor Gratarol”. First-person memoir and defence in Italian, with appended letters. Raw text: 10,354 lines (Columbia University Library copy).
The continuation and conclusion of Gratarol’s vindication. Parte Seconda takes up his story where Parte Prima left it — his departure from Venice — and carries it through his years of exile, ending in the collection of documentary letters that vindicate his memory. This third edition appends the Riflessioni d’un Imparziale (“Reflections of an Impartial [Observer]”) preceded by a further letter from Gratarol.
Contents
The narrative of Parte Seconda opens with Gratarol’s departure from Venice. He describes his retreat to Padua — too close to Venice not to feel the separation — where, in greater freedom, he set his affairs in order and meditated on the future. He then resolves to make his way first toward Brunswick, soliciting by letter the protection of its Serene Duke Ferdinand, and to revisit Ceneda among his old friends before quitting his native region.
From this point the Parte Seconda follows the course of his exile. He relates his journey across the Alps and through the German courts, his reception, his correspondence, and his final arrival at Stockholm in March, where he settled and where, in 1779, his Narrazione Apologetica was first printed (in quarto, at the press of Fougt). He reflects on the conspiracies, libels and calumnies that continued to pursue him even in exile, and answers at length the charges and pamphlets circulated against him — including attacks in the Venetian and Cisalpine press.
The appended Riflessioni d’un Imparziale (beginning mid-volume) offer an independent commentary on the affair and Gratarol’s conduct, followed by a substantial collection of letters documenting his later life and vindication: letters between Gratarol and his correspondents, including the English gentleman Mr. Morton Pitt, the Baron Enrico d’Adelsheim, Orazio Lavezzari, and others, exchanged through 1787–1792.
These final letters record the melancholy close of the affair — Gratarol’s imprisonment and his death — and testify to how his reputation was regarded by his friends after his death. The volume ends with the words Il Fine, closing the apologia as a whole.

sources/hazlitt-venetian-republic-comple.title: Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic (Complete Single-Volume Edition)
sources/hazlitt-venetian-republic-comple.content:
Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic (Complete Single-Volume Edition)
Full Title: The Venetian Republic: Its Rise, Its Growth, and Its Fall, A.D. 409-1797
Author: William Carew Hazlitt (1834–1913)
Publisher: Likely the enlarged/revised single-volume edition (1915 or later reprint) — distributed as an ACLS Humanities E-Book
Source: EPUB file, 1,050 HTML pages. Raw text: 11,577 lines, born-digital (no OCR artifacts).
This single-volume edition includes the full text of both Volumes I and II. Notably, it contains Chapters XXIX, XXX, and XXXI which cover the period 1423–1457 — the gap missing from the two separate volume zips.
Chapters XXIX–XXXI (the missing chapters)
These three chapters bridge the gap between the original Vol. I (ending at Chapter XXVIII, 1431) and Vol. II (starting at Chapter XXXII, 1457):
CHAPTER XXIX — A.D. 1423–1431 (p. 855)
Francesco Carmagnola enters Venetian service — League between Florence and Venice — fall of Brescia — Battle of Macalo — peace and cession of Bergamo to Venice — third war against Milan.
CHAPTER XXX — A.D. 1431–1441 (p. 892)
Arrest and execution of Carmagnola — Peace of 1433 — Cosimo de’ Medici at Venice — Francesco Sforza becomes Captain-General — successes of 1440 — Peace of 1441 — marriage of Jacopo Foscari — Venice acquires Ravenna.
CHAPTER XXXI — A.D. 1441–1457 (p. 935)
Death of Filippo-Maria Visconti (1447) — War of the Succession — Sforza becomes Duke of Milan — Treaty of Lodi (1454) — Fall of Constantinople (1453) — Treaty between Venice and Mehmed II — Story of the Two Foscari — deposition and death of Doge Foscari (1457).
Relevance
This EPUB is the source for the three missing chapters. The original Vol. I zip (1900 edition) only goes to Chapter XXVIII, and the original Vol. II zip (AMS Press reprint) starts at Chapter XXXII. This EPUB fills that 26-year gap.

sources/hazlitt_venetian_republic_vol1.title: William Carew Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic: Its Rise, Its Growth, and Its Fall (Vol. I)
sources/hazlitt_venetian_republic_vol1.content:
Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic, Vol. I (1900)
Full Title: The Venetian Republic: Its Rise, Its Growth, and Its Fall
Author: William Carew Hazlitt (1834–1913)
Publisher: A. & C. Black, London, 1900
Source: Anna’s Archive / Harvard College Library scan (OCLC 7075165). 850 page-image text files in sources/32044105539571/.
Line Count: ~2,053,000 characters across 850 pages.
This is the first volume of Hazlitt’s comprehensive history of Venice. It traces the Republic from its origins in the lagoon settlements (409 AD) through the consolidation of its constitution, its rise as a Mediterranean maritime power, the Crusades, the struggle with Genoa, the War of Chioggia, and the acquisition of a mainland empire — ending at 1431 with the reign of Doge Francesco Foscari and the acquisition of Saloniki.
The work draws heavily on Romanin’s Storia Documentata di Venezia and the Calendar of Venetian State Papers, as well as the diaries of Marino Sanuto and other contemporary sources. Hazlitt frames Venice’s political structure as “perfectly unparalleled” and treats its 14-century lifespan as a dramatic arc from rise to zenith to dissolution.
The 15th and 16th centuries (the period of Venice’s peak power and gradual decline) are covered in the subsequent volumes, which are not present in this archive.
Contents
CHAPTER I — A.D. 409–654 (p. 1)
Venetia Princeps — Successive rulers of the mainland. The earliest lagoon settlements, the formation of the Venetian people from refugees fleeing barbarian invasions, and the first rudimentary constitutions.
CHAPTER II — A.D. 654–787 (p. 17)
Tribunitial government abolished — establishment of the dogeship — vicissitudes of the office. Military constitution of Venice, the first Italian treaty, and the Republic’s first belligerent actions.
CHAPTER III — A.D. 787–809 (p. 31)
Internal discord — balancing policy between the Greeks and Franks — defeat of the Frankish forces in 809. The rivalry of Heraclia and Malamocco.
CHAPTER IV — A.D. 809–864 (p. 46)
The Badoer dynasty — commencement of architectural improvements — continuance of civil war — growth of power. A doge seeks the cloister.
CHAPTER V — A.D. 864–912 (p. 59)
Schism with the Holy See — financial schemes — fall of a doge in battle — rise of the House of Sanudo — first continental acquisition at Terra Firma — the Huns again in Italy.
CHAPTER VI — A.D. 912–991 (p. 73)
Brides of St. Mark — fall of the Sanudo dynasty — succession of the Orseoli — a doge turns monk.
CHAPTER VII — A.D. 991–1084 (p. 103)
The Orseolo dynasty — submission of Dalmatia — constitutional reforms — the Northmen.
CHAPTER VIII — A.D. 1084–1128 (p. 141)
The Faliero and Michieli dynasties — the Crusades — Venetian accessions in the Levant — the doge at Jerusalem.
CHAPTER IX — A.D. 1128–1172 (p. 176)
Important relations and alliances — farther operations in Sicily and Greece — the Lombard League.
CHAPTER X — A.D. 1173–1201 (p. 205)
Constitutional and official developments — creation of the Great Council — participation in the Fifth Crusade.
CHAPTER XI — A.D. 1202–1205 (p. 246)
Departure for Constantinople — the Fifth Crusade — the voyage to Constantinople — arrival there — trials and perils.
CHAPTER XII — A.D. 1203–1205 (p. 279)
Fall of Constantinople — election of a new emperor — partition of the Empire — the Republic’s large share in the conquest.
CHAPTER XIII — A.D. 1205–1229 (p. 310)
A new era — difficulties regarding possessions — early decline of the Latin power at Constantinople — the Jubilee of 1214 — Venetian colonisation — a startling proposal.
CHAPTER XIV — A.D. 1229–1249 (p. 341)
Increasing political prominence of Venice in European affairs — pawn of the Crown of Thorns — the Republic and the German Empire.
CHAPTER XV — A.D. 1249–1268 (p. 362)
Troubles in the East — hostilities with Genoa — Padua and the Eccelini — legal reforms.
CHAPTER XVI — A.D. 1268–1280 (p. 398)
Institution of the Chancery — festivities at a coronation — declaration of sovereignty over the Adriatic.
CHAPTER XVII — A.D. 1280–1289 (p. 424)
A republican doge elected — formation of a league against Venice — the Sicilian Vespers — the Holy Office at Venice — the first gold ducat.
CHAPTER XVIII — A.D. 1289–1302 (p. 442)
War with Genoa and the Greek emperor — severe reverses of the Republic — Marco Polo — return of peace in 1302.
CHAPTER XIX — A.D. 1286–1309 (p. 474)
Constitutional agitation — Serrar del Gran Consiglio — rupture with the Pope — interdict of 1309.
CHAPTER XX — A.D. 1310–1311 (p. 517)
The Quirini-Tiepolo conspiracy — establishment of a temporary Committee of Public Safety (Council of Ten) — institution of a police.
CHAPTER XXI — A.D. 1311–1342 (p. 537)
Venetian prosperity — relations with European and Asiatic powers — Council of Ten made a permanent assembly — acquisition of Treviso.
CHAPTER XXII — A.D. 1343–1354 (p. 569)
Active military and naval operations — severe struggle with Genoa — Petrarch.
CHAPTER XXIII — A.D. 1354–1355 (p. 592)
Continuation of the Genoese war — story of Marino Faliero.
CHAPTER XXIV — A.D. 1355–1365 (p. 614)
Hostilities with Genoa and Hungary — trouble in Candia (Crete) — a doge with a taste for horses and a dislike to interference.
CHAPTER XXV — A.D. 1365–1378 (p. 643)
Last days of Petrarch — his gift to Venice — growth of a coalition against the Republic between Austria and other powers — Sir John Hawkwood.
CHAPTER XXVI — A.D. 1378–1383 (p. 669)
The War of Chioggia — a fight for life — Venice ultimately triumphant — romantic details.
CHAPTER XXVII — A.D. 1383–1413 (p. 718)
Decline of Genoa — important accessions of Italian territory to Venice — rise of the Osmanli (Ottomans) and of the House of Visconti — great achievements of Carlo Zeno.
CHAPTER XXVIII — A.D. 1414–1431 (p. 785)
The Pacific Doge Mocenigo — death of Carlo Zeno — operations against the Emperor Sigismund — extensive gains of territory in the Levant — acquisition of Saloniki.

END OF VOL. I — Subsequent volumes continue through the 15th, 16th, and 17th centuries to the Republic’s fall in 1797.

sources/hazlitt_venetian_republic_vol2.title: William Carew Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic: Its Rise, Its Growth, and Its Fall (Vol. II)
sources/hazlitt_venetian_republic_vol2.content:
Hazlitt — The Venetian Republic, Vol. II (AMS Press reprint, 1966)
Full Title: The Venetian Republic: Its Rise, Its Growth, and Its Fall, A.D. 409-1797 — Volume II (1457-1797)
Author: William Carew Hazlitt (1834–1913)
Publisher: AMS Press, New York, 1966 (reprint of the 1915 edition by Adam and Charles Black, London)
Source: UCSD Library scan from the New York Public Library collections. 1,130 page-image text files in sources-ams/31822005854989/.
Line Count: ~2,844,000 characters across 1,130 pages.
This is the second and final volume of Hazlitt’s comprehensive history of Venice. It covers the Republic’s history from 1457 to its final dissolution in 1797, followed by 25 thematic chapters on Venetian civilization, government, economy, culture, and daily life. The volume includes plates, maps, corrigenda, and a full index.
The 15th and 16th century chapters (XXXII-XXXVI) cover Venice’s peak maritime power — the acquisition of Cyprus, the League of Cambrai, the Battle of Agnadello, the recovery of Padua, the Battle of Marignano, the Battle of Lepanto, and the Interdict controversy with Pope Paul V — as well as cultural figures like Titian, Paolo Sarpi, and Bianca Cappello.
Contents
NARRATIVE HISTORY (Chapters XXXII-XLI)
CHAPTER XXXII — A.D. 1457–1501 (p. 1)
Venice in the mid-15th century — Dominio Veneto replaces Commune Venetiarum — the Turks at Constantinople — a new crusade organized and abandoned (1464) — succession of Doges (1462–1501) — the Fire of 1479 — quarrel with the Holy See over Ferrara — interdict — acquisition of Cyprus — Caterina Cornaro’s last days — geographical discoveries and Venetian anxiety — the French in Italy — the Holy League — Ludovico il Moro — Battle of Sapienza (1499) — Venetian defeat.
CHAPTER XXXIII — A.D. 1501–1509 (p. 38)
Leonardo Loredano, Doge — formation of a European coalition against Venice — League of Cambrai — friendly feeling of Henry VIII toward Venice — his diplomatic offices at the Vatican — offers of help from Scotland and Spain — Henry VIII and the Venetian ambassador — Cardinal Wolsey’s interviews with the Venetian envoy.
CHAPTER XXXIV — A.D. 1509–1529 (p. 50)
The League of Cambrai — vigilance and activity of the Republic — defeat at Agnadello — arrival of the intelligence at Venice — launch of the Interdict by Julius II — fortitude of the Government — the Doge sends his plate to the Mint — recovery of Padua (17 July 1509) — repulse of Emperor Maximilian — defection of Julius II — Leo X (1513) — reconciliation with France — Battle of Marignano decided by the Venetians (1515) — Charles V — Battle of Pavia (1525) — Italian League against the Emperor (1526) — sack of Rome (1527) — Treaty of Cambrai (1529) — obstacles to Italian unity.
CHAPTER XXXV — A.D. 1521–1573 (p. 94)
Death of Leonardo Loredano (1521) — splendid funeral — Andrea Gritti, Doge (1523–38) — Turkey and Egypt — absorption of Egypt by the Porte — plague and famine — convalescent homes — Gritti’s architectural improvements — Council of Trent — Protestantism and Elizabeth of England — explosion of the Venetian powder magazine at the Arsenal (1569) — loss of Cyprus (1570) — Battle of Lepanto (1571) — rejoicings at Venice — peace with Turkey (1573).
CHAPTER XXXVI — A.D. 1545–1607 (p. 127)
Sequence of Doges (1545–77) — Henry III of France at Venice (1574) — his magnificent reception — plague of 1576 and death of Titian — the Pope sends the Golden Rose — great Fire of 1577 — loss of treasures — story of Bianca Cappello as Grand Duchess of Tuscany — quarrel with Pope Paul V (1605–07) — Fra Paolo Sarpi appointed Canonist and Ritualistic Adviser (1606) — European sympathy with Venice — Interdict and its withdrawal — triumph of the Republic over the Curia — James I and his Apology for the Oath of Allegiance (1607) — plot to assassinate Sarpi.
CHAPTER XXXVII — A.D. 1607–1623 (p. 160)
Spanish Conspiracy against Venice (1618) — long and secret preparations — the city full of traitors and bravoes — denunciation to the Signory — wholesale arrests — 300 executions — French and Spanish ambassadors leave Venice — death of Ossuna — case of Antonio Foscarini (1622) — Lady Arundel and Sir Henry Wotton — mistake of the Council of Ten — death of Paolo Sarpi (1623).
CHAPTER XXXVIII — A.D. 1623–1669 (p. 201)
Rialto Bridge erected (1588) — Doge Bembo — Reniero Zeno’s attacks on the Council of Ten (1624–28) — Venice and the Netherlands — War in the Valtelline (1620) — plague at Venice (1630) — deaths of Richelieu and Louis XIII (1642–43) — Candiot War (1644–69) — strenuous exertions to preserve Crete — Treaty of Westphalia (1648) — eventual surrender of Candia to the Porte on honourable terms.
CHAPTER XXXIX — A.D. 1669–1699 (p. 240)
Operations in the Morea under Francesco Morosini — successes — election of Morosini to the Dogeship (1688) — his death at Napoli di Romania (1694) — victories over the Turks at Zenta by Prince Eugene (1697) — Peace of Carlowitz (1699).
CHAPTER XL — A.D. 1699–1762 (p. 263)
War of the Spanish Succession — Venetian neutrality — loss of the Morea — Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) — Venice adopts permanent neutrality — relaxation of customs tariff (1736) — “a great Empire reduced to a great City” — Clement XIII, a Venetian, becomes Pope (1758).
CHAPTER XLI — A.D. 1762–1797 (p. 284)
Marco Foscarini, Doge (1762–63) — Angelo Emo’s triumphs at sea (1784–92) — case of Pier Antonio Gratarol — Paolo Renier and Luigi Manin, the last Doges (1779–97) — approach of the end — the French in Italy — negotiations of Procurator Pietro Pesaro with Bonaparte — last act of the Venetian Senate (1797) — surrender of the city to the French — the 120th Doge abdicates.
SUPPLEMENTARY / THEMATIC CHAPTERS (Chapters XLII-LXVI)
CHAPTER XLII (p. 307) — The Foundations
Primeval Venice — the letters of Cassiodorus (520–23) — the original walled city — the Abbey of San Zaccaria.
CHAPTER XLIII (p. 325) — The Choice of a Capital
Rialto as ultimate Venice (809) — thoroughfares — bridges — Saint Mark’s as a feudal fortress — paving of the Broglio — open spaces (campi) — earliest places of business.
CHAPTER XLIV (p. 345) — The Fortified City
Venice as a fortified city — the Palazzi — the Ducal Palace — the Horses of Saint Mark.
CHAPTER XLV (p. 375) — The Church
Origin and rise of the Church — Grado and Aquileia — translation of Saint Mark (829) — establishment of the Holy Office (1289) — Venetian toleration — first Patriarch of Venice (1454).
CHAPTER XLVI (p. 412) — The Doge
Attributes of the office — the Promission — the Ducal Palace — bodyguard — ceremonial — the trumpets, tapers, sword of State and Umbrella.
CHAPTER XLVII (p. 431) — Election of Doges
Election in 1071 described — coronation of the Dogaressa — obsequies — the Bucentaurs.
CHAPTER XLVIII (p. 448) — Government by Departments
The College, Great Council, Senate, Council of Ten — the Inquisition of State (1539) — the completed Constitution.
CHAPTER XLIX (p. 484) — Magistracies
Procurators of Saint Mark — Avogadors — Grand Chancellor — public records — fires of 1479, 1483, 1574, 1577 — Marino Sanudo’s itinerary of 1483.
CHAPTER L (p. 532) — The Navy
Organization — the Arsenal (referenced in Dante’s Inferno) — Venetian shipwrights for Peter the Great (1698) — Venetian militia.
CHAPTER LI (p. 557) — The Laws
The Statuto of 1242 — maritime insurance — the Nautical Capitulary.
CHAPTER LII (p. 578) — Police and Prisons
Signori di Notte — the Piombi — the Bravo system.
CHAPTER LIII (p. 618) — Feudal System
Forms of tenure — villanage — serfdom — Montaigne as a witness — Venetian courtesans.
CHAPTER LIV (p. 648) — Commerce
Postal system — annual trading fleets — the Flanders voyage — Southampton — Venice and England (Edward I to Henry IV).
CHAPTER LV (p. 696) — Trade Gilds
Painters, tapissers, carpenters, masons — glass furnaces — spectacles.
CHAPTER LVI (p. 713) — Industries
Organ-building — bells — clocks — earthenware — lace — Fondaco dei Tedeschi — Compagnia della Calza.
CHAPTER LVII (p. 731) — Coinage
First gold ducat (1284) — scudo d’oro (1528–30) — the Giustina (1571).
CHAPTER LVIII (p. 768) — Finance
Chamber of Loans — Monte Vecchio and Monte Nuovo — Bank of Venice — rent-rolls (1365–1425).
CHAPTER LIX (p. 780) — Arts and Sciences
Geographical knowledge — Marco Polo — Marino Sanudo — the Zeni — John and Sebastian Cabot — the mariner’s compass.
CHAPTER LX (p. 808) — Education
Private tutors — the Venetian dialect — great families — University of Padua — Galileo.
CHAPTER LXI (p. 829) — Literature
Historical literature — Paolo Sarpi — the “Admirable Crichton” — folk rhymes.
CHAPTER LXII (p. 859) — Drama and Printing
Gregorio Corraro — first theatres — Evelyn at the opera — female writers — Marcian Library — origin of printing: the Spiras, Jenson, Aldus Manutius.
CHAPTER LXIII (p. 896) — Domestic Life
The Venetian house — water supply — plagues and famines — Board of Health — quarantine.
CHAPTER LXIV (p. 926) — Hospitals and Manners
Charities — costume — chopines (zilve) — Pietro Casola at Venice in 1494 — sumptuary laws — the gondoliers.
CHAPTER LXV (p. 975) — Meals and Amusements
Diet and provisions — games — music — painting — Titian’s circle — Pietro Aretino — Giorgione — the Bellini — Paolo Veronese — Canova.
CHAPTER LXVI (p. 997) — Later Venetian Life
Luxury — the Regatta — the Carnival — masks — gaming — Ridotti — Café Florian — street music — country houses.
Back matter: Corrigenda, Index, Plates

sources/lane-venice-maritime-republic.title: Lane — Venice, A Maritime Republic
sources/lane-venice-maritime-republic.content:
Venice, A Maritime Republic
Frederic Chapin Lane, Venice, A Maritime Republic (Baltimore & London: The Johns Hopkins University Press, 1973). 526 pages. ISBN 0-8018-1445-6 (cloth), 0-8018-1460-X (pbk.). Raw text: 32,490 lines.
A classic comprehensive survey of Venetian history focused on its maritime and commercial character. Lane (1900–1984), one of the preeminent historians of medieval and Renaissance Venice, traces the Republic from its origins in the lagoons through its rise as a naval power, its commercial empire, its constitutional development, and its eventual decline and fall.
The book is organized thematically within a chronological framework, with chapters on navigation, trade, shipbuilding, naval warfare, politics, and the Venetian economy. Lane draws on extensive archival research to provide a rounded portrait of Venice as a “maritime republic” whose power derived from the sea.
Contents
Preface (p. vii) | Chronology (p. xvi)
INTRODUCTORY
1. The Beginnings (p. 1) — The first Venetians; trade and navigation on the rivers; the turn seaward.
2. The Port-City and Its Population (p. 10) — Integration of communities; a safe harbor; population figures and the plague.
THE CONQUEST OF SEA POWER
3. Police and Piracy in the Adriatic (p. 22)
4. Victories Beyond-the-Sea and in Romania (p. 30) — The First Crusades; the Fourth Crusade; an empire of naval bases.
THE ORGANIZATION OF SEA POWER
5. Ships, Crews, and the Ship’s Company (p. 44) — Ships and navigation; seamen and traveling merchants.
6. The Lordship of the Gulf (p. 56) — Salt, wheat, and the hinterland; the transit trade; the War of Ferrara.
7. The Trade of the Levant (p. 66) — Caravans over sea and land; Genoese rivalry; the Mongols and new trade routes.
ARISTOCRATIC POLITY
8. From Dukedom to Commune (p. 86) — Myth and reality in the dukedom; doges within a commune; the constitutional framework.
9. The Growing Structure of the Commune (p. 102) — Guilds and the little people; restraint of faction; enlargement of the Great Council; conspiracy and the Council of Ten.
A REORGANIZATION OF SEA POWER
10. The Response to the Nautical Revolution of the Middle Ages (p. 118) — New techniques; convoys and their protection; free voyaging.
11. The Commercial Revolution of the Resident Merchants (p. 136) — Business organization; cartels; usury and finance; grosso and ducat; the public debt.
12. Craftsmen and Seamen (p. 154) — Industrial organization; chemicals, textiles, and construction; guild functions; a proletariat among seamen.
TRIUMPH BY COHESION
13. Symptoms of Disintegration (p. 172) — The Third Genoese War; Andrea Dandolo; Marino Falier; two decades of doubt.
14. The Climax of the Struggle with Genoa (p. 188) — The War of Chioggia; regaining lost ground.
THE TURN WESTWARD
15. Arts, Sciences, and Literature (p. 202) — Byzantine and Gothic; the painters; scientists and humanists; early Renaissance architecture.
16. Contests for Power: The Fifteenth Century (p. 224) — Expansion on the mainland; condottieri and the balance of power in Italy; the Ottoman Turks in the balance; the most triumphant city.
17. Contests for Power: The Sixteenth Century (p. 240) — The turning point; the League of Cambrai; a second-class sea power; the turning point reconsidered.
18. The Corruption and Perfection of the Constitution (p. 250) — Noble gentlemen, sovereign and equal; the organs of government; practical politics; administration and the doges; the consent of the governed.
THE OCEANIC CHALLENGE
19. Participants in Oceanic Discoveries (p. 274) — Map makers; explorers and their narratives.
20. The Spice Trade (p. 284) — Exploiting the Red Sea route; Portuguese competition; competitors after 1570.
21. The Shifts in Other Trades (p. 296) — Colonial products and bullion; Levantine merchants, Jews, and the ghettos; new markets; food and the grain trade.
22. The Expansion of Manufactures (p. 308) — Old industries and new; craftsmen and capitalists; the role of the guilds.
23. Finance and Income from Power (p. 322) — Government jobs; public finance; giro-banks, private and public; rich and poor.
CHANGING FLEETS AND SHIPYARDS
24. The Peak and Passing of the Merchant Galleys (p. 336) — Expansion; management and regulation; crews and passengers; their final voyages.
25. The War Fleets (p. 354) — New foes and new weapons; naval administration and the Arsenal; crews and their commanders; Lepanto and after.
26. Argosies with Portly Sails (p. 376) — Timber shortage, falling freights, and subsidies; caracks ascendant; the collapse.
A TENACIOUS DEFENSE
27. Of Sovereignty and the Constitution (p. 390) — Peace-keeping diplomacy; embryonic parties; an interdict defied; the Hapsburg vise; economic downturn; stagnation in politics.
28. In a New Age of Sea Power (p. 406) — The new pattern; the last Turkish wars; ships, commanders, and crews; the loss of Adriatic lordship; revivals in merchant shipping.
29. The Death of the Republic (p. 422) — An economy not in decline; the apex of oligarchy; a stop on the Grand Tour; last days.
30. The Completion and Preservation of the City (p. 438) — The High Renaissance; the Late Renaissance and after; leadership in painting; the lagoon; the perils now.
Bibliographical Notes (p. 459) | Index (p. 485)
Relevance to Venice Wiki
Lane is arguably the single most authoritative modern survey of Venetian history covering the 15th–16th centuries. Chapters 16–20 are directly relevant to the folder’s focus: the 15th–16th century Venetian state in its maritime context, including the League of Cambrai, the maritime challenge from the Ottomans and Portuguese, the spice trade, and Oceanic discoveries.

sources/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.title: Lowry — The World of Aldus Manutius
sources/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.content:
The World of Aldus Manutius: Business and Scholarship in Renaissance Venice
Martin Lowry, The World of Aldus Manutius: Business and Scholarship in Renaissance Venice (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1979). 376 pages. ISBN 9780801412141. Raw text: 18,338 lines.
A scholarly monograph on Aldus Manutius (1450–1515) and the Aldine Press, examining the relationship between Renaissance scholarship and commercial printing. Lowry analyzes the structure of the Aldine firm, its output during Aldus’s lifetime, and changes in its business and editorial policies. He draws on archival materials and press copies to offer a revision of Aldus’s accepted position in the history of the printed book.
Contents
Introduction (pp. 1–8): Scope and methodology.
Ch. 1 — Men of Business and Men of Letters (pp. 9–48): The Venetian printing world before Aldus — John of Speyer, Nicolas Jenson, and the early Venetian printer-publishers. The economics of early printing in Venice.
Ch. 2 — The Wandering Scholar (pp. 49–90): Aldus’s early life and education — studies in Rome and Ferrara, tutoring of the Pio princes of Carpi, Greek studies under Guarini and Adramyttenos, the plan to print Greek classics.
Ch. 3 — Barbarigo, Torresani and Manuzio (pp. 91–128): Founding of the Aldine Press — financial backers (Pierfrancesco Barbarigo, Andrea Torresani), marriage to Torresani’s daughter Maria, merger of the Jenson-Torresani printing office with Aldus’s new press.
Ch. 4 — The Chances of Business (pp. 129–168): Practical operations — production methods, typefounding, paper supply, labor relations, edition sizes, pricing, distribution. The Greek type and the italic type (Francesco Griffo). Piratical competition from Lyons. Privileges.
Ch. 5 — Academic Dreams (pp. 169–208): The Aldine Academy (Neacademia) and its scholarly program. Greek refugee scholars. Editorial methods for the Greek classics. The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499).
Ch. 6 — Authorship and Editorship (pp. 209–248): Relationships with authors and editors — Erasmus, Bembo, Musurus, Navagero. The role of the corrector. Transition from scholarly editing to commercial publishing.
Ch. 7 — The Great Diffusion (pp. 249–288): Spread of Aldine books across Europe — distribution networks, book fairs, agents. Influence of Aldine typography on other printers (Estiennes, Froben, Elzevirs). The octavo revolution.
Conclusion (pp. 289–304): Assessment of Aldus’s place in printing history. Commerce and scholarship. The Aldine legacy.
Appendices, Bibliography, Index (pp. 305–376).
Relevance to Venice Wiki
Covers the Aldine Press as a Venetian institution — its business structure, its place in Venetian commerce, its network of scholars and patrons in Renaissance Venice, and its competition with other Venetian printers (especially the Jenson-Torresani interests). Essential for understanding Venice as a center of Renaissance printing and scholarship.

sources/mueller-venetian-money-market.title: Mueller — The Venetian Money Market
sources/mueller-venetian-money-market.content:
The Venetian Money Market: Banks, Panics, and the Public Debt, 1200–1500
Reinhold C. Mueller, The Venetian Money Market: Banks, Panics, and the Public Debt, 1200–1500. Volume II of Money and Banking in Medieval and Renaissance Venice (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2019, open access edition). 726 pages. ISBN 978-1-4214-3142-0 (electronic). Raw text: 36,950 lines, born-digital.
This is the second volume of the landmark study of Venetian financial institutions. Volume I — Coins and Moneys of Account (1985) — was co-authored by Frederic C. Lane and Reinhold C. Mueller. Mueller, a student of Lane’s and a leading scholar of Venetian economic history, wrote this volume independently. It provides the definitive treatment of the private banking system, the public debt (Monte Vecchio), and the foreign exchange market that made Venice the financial capital of late medieval Europe.
The book traces the evolution of the Venetian money market from the rise of deposit banking at the Rialto in the 13th century through the crises of the 14th and 15th centuries, the consolidation of the Monte Vecchio system, and the sophisticated exchange market that connected Venice to the business centres of Europe.
Contents
PART I — Local Banks and Bankers: The Institutional Side (5 chapters)
1. From Moneychanging to Deposit Banking — The Rialto banks, bank money (banco di scritta), the role of moneychangers, literary evidence from Sanudo and Pacioli.
2. The Bankers — The social and economic background of Venetian bankers. Noble, citizen, and foreign bankers. The Soranzo, the Garzoni, the Lippomano families.
3. The Structure of Banking — Banking regulation. The Ufficiali sopra i banchi. Reserve requirements. The prohibition of speculative banking.
4. Bank Failures — Anatomy of a bank failure. The panics of 1401, 1415, 1456, 1498, 1500. Government intervention. The Bank of the Rialto.
5. Forms of Business Organization and Liability — Partnerships (fraterna, compagnia). Limited and unlimited liability. The role of notaries.
6. Proposals for a Public Bank — Debates over the creation of a state bank. The Banco Giro (1619). Earlier proposals in the 15th century.
PART II — Local Banks in Action: The Documentary Side (2 chapters)
7. The Case of the Garzoni Bank — A detailed micro-history of a single bank: its rise, operations, and failure through archival records.
8. The Soranzo Fraterna — A family partnership in banking. The Soranzo bank’s records, clients, and transactions.
PART III — The Exchange Market (3 chapters)
9. The Grain Office and the Exchange — The intersection of grain provisioning and foreign exchange. Public finance and the exchange rate.
10. Bank Loans to the State — How banks lent to the Venetian government. Camerlenghi loans. Short-term credit.
11. Parties to a Bill of Exchange — The mechanics of the bill of exchange. Venetian merchants and the fairs of Geneva, Bruges, and beyond. Usury and the canon law.
12. The Exchange with London and the Low Countries — Venetian bills on London and Bruges. The Priuli fraterna’s operations. Exchange rates and market conditions.
13. The Exchange with the Levant — Venetian bills on Constantinople, Alexandria, and the Black Sea. The problem of transferring funds across the Mediterranean.
PART IV — The Market in Government Securities (2 chapters)
14. Family and Finance: Forced Loans and the Open Market — The Monte Vecchio system in action. Speculation and prices. The Andrea Barbarigo case study. Demand and supply of prestiti.
15. Investment by Foreigners in the Monte Vecchio — International investors in Venetian public debt. Foreign lords and courtiers. Reprisals and portfolio management.
PART V — Conclusion and Appendices
Conclusion (p. 568) — Synthesis of the Venetian money market’s evolution.
Appendix A — Local Deposit Bankers and Partnerships (chronological listing, p. 579)
Appendix B — Failures of Local Deposit Banks (p. 584)
Appendix C — Foreign Exchange in Venice during the Datini Years, 1383–1410 (p. 587)
Appendix D — Moneys of Account Revisited (p. 610)
Appendix E — Foreign Investors in Venetian Credit Institutions (p. 626)
Relevance to Venice Wiki
This is the definitive source for all financial topics already covered in the wiki: the Banco Giro, the Monte Vecchio system, the Rialto banks, bills of exchange, marine insurance, and public finance. It significantly expands the existing venetian-coinage-and-finance concept page and adds depth to commercial-revolution, constitutional-development, the-condottieri-system (which discusses war finance), and the events pages that touch on fiscal crises. The detailed case studies (Garzoni, Soranzo, Priuli, Barbarigo) provide a micro-historical dimension that Lane’s broader survey lacks.

sources/spada-memorie-apologetiche-parte.title: Spada — Memorie Apologetiche, Parte Prima
sources/spada-memorie-apologetiche-parte.content:
Memorie Apologetiche di Giovanni Andrea Spada — Parte Prima
Giovanni Andrea Spada, Memorie Apologetiche scritte da lui medesimo (Brescia, 1801), Part I. First-person memoir in Italian. Raw text: 2,081 lines (heavily OCR-garbled 1801 printing; long-s and broken word-spacing throughout).
An apologia (defense) written by a Venetian citizen who held office in the provisional administration that governed Venice in the months after the fall of the Republic. Spada writes to clear his name against the charge — spread by libellists after the Austro-French settlement — that he and a small group of collaborators had single-handedly betrayed and destroyed the Venetian Republic.
Contents
The volume opens with the fall of the Republic itself. Spada describes the mood in Venice on the eve of the Austrian occupation of 1798: how nobles, the ministry, the troops, the merchants and even the clergy, for their own separate reasons, had come to desire the arrival of the Austrians; and how the so-called congiura del Cercato (the “conspiracy of the Cercato”), the policies of the municipality and the conduct of France had all disposed the Venetian people to welcome a change of regime. He recounts the triumphant entry of General Wallis — the reception that Spada himself, as a member of the municipal government, helped organise — and marks the moment as the one in which Venice, once free and sovereign, became the last subject city of Francis II.
Spada then explains the new provisional administration of which he was a member. He traces the decree (January 1798) that concentrated the authority of a provisional government in a council of ten — Bujovich, Dolfin, and others — and describes how each deputy took charge of a department; his own was finance. He gives an account of the state of the Venetian treasury the administration found on taking office, the tasks of restoring the salt tax (ferma of salt) and provisioning the Austrian troops, and the running of the mint and the banco giro.
The memoir moves to the final acts of the Venetian state. Spada narrates the delicate matter of the oath of fidelity to Francis II, the resistance of the old patriciate, the last session of the Maggior Consiglio (Great Council) in February 1798 — called without the doge and the usual authorities, and so, by the ancient laws, illegitimate — the role of Giovan Pietro Grimani as the last ambassador to Vienna, and the ceremony in which the delegates swore homage, fidelity and obedience to the Emperor as head of the House of Austria-Lorraine.
The later chapters are Spada’s defence and record of persecution. He answers the accusation that a handful of men (naming Morosini, the Doge Manin, Pisan, Sanfermo, Foscarini, and himself) had engineered the Republic’s fall, insisting that the alleged conspiracy never existed and that the sacking of 12 May was the work of incitement and the neglect of certain magistrates. He recounts how, in his zeal for the Erario (the public treasury) and the preservation of the patria, he proposed reforms that brought him into conflict with the powerful Pesaros; how he was denounced, accused of conspiracy in favour of Austria, and thrown with his son into the Piombi (the lead-roofed state prisons) by the Inquisitori di Stato (State Inquisitors); and how he was then held for months at San Giorgio, later led under guard from Padua to Verona, where he was told of his perpetual exile and escorted to the banks of the Mincio.
The memoir closes with the Conclusione a tutta l’opera — Spada’s summary of his misfortunes, his declaration that he never took part in any decree of spoliation and always defended his family against the Inquisitors of State, his account of the death of his son (whom the tyrant Molin forbade him to embrace as he lay dying in April 1800), and an impassioned appeal to Italy to lay aside her Guelf and Ghibelline factions and unite for her independence.

sources/spada-memorie-apologetiche-parte.title: Spada — Memorie Apologetiche, Parte Seconda
sources/spada-memorie-apologetiche-parte.content:
Memorie Apologetiche di Giovanni Andrea Spada — Parte Seconda
Giovanni Andrea Spada, Memorie Apologetiche scritte da lui medesimo (Brescia, 1801), Part II. First-person memoir in Italian. Raw text: 3,440 lines (Harvard College Library copy, cleaner OCR than the Parts I & III scan).
The middle part of Spada’s apologia. Where Part I set out the author’s account of the fall of the Republic and his own persecution and exile, Part II narrows to his conduct during the municipal regime — the months between the abdication of the Great Council in May 1797 and the establishment of the Austrian provisional government — when Spada served as a member of the provisional municipality, chiefly in charge of finance.
Contents
The Introduzione opens on 16 May 1797, when the provisional municipality was installed in Venice. Spada insists that the change of government came about not by revolution or any internal conspiracy but in virtue of a solemn renunciation, itself the consequence of the events of war and of the reckless directions of a senate he calls imbecile and deceived by its leaders. He describes the municipality as a body formed by chance, of men almost all at odds in principles and objects, and sets out his intent to render an account of his own conduct alone.
Chapter I — On the Amnesty promised in the abdication of the Maggior Consiglio. Spada defends the pledge of amnesty given when the Great Council laid down its sovereignty, and attacks those who, in a spirit of party, sought to subvert it. He reflects on how every Venetian was educated under the weight of terror, on the servitude of the clergy to the Senate, and on the abuse of that solemn promise by his enemies — a theme that runs through his whole defence.
Chapter II — Finance. Spada turns to the ruinous state of the Venetian treasury. He recounts how the state was loaded with funded capital of over 43 million ducats bearing an annual charge of more than a million and a half; how the war against Tunis had cost over a million zecchini in troop pay and equipment sent to Cavalier Emo; how the Procurator Pesaro’s new customs plan, sustained against the Savio Battaggia, had wasted some 80,000 ducats and diminished the annual revenue; and how the economy, unbalanced in its basis, suffered daily shocks from disorder. He defends his own conduct in charge of the finances against the charge of arbitrariness, insisting he refused every personal advantage and enforced rigour in the public interest.
Chapter III — On the peace treaty with France, and the political directions of the municipality. Spada recounts the municipality’s negotiations and its policy towards the French peace — the treaty that he maintains saved to Venice its political representation — and defends the line he took in upholding the sacred title of that treaty against his enemies, who had accused him of conspiring in favour of Austria.
Chapter IV — The Office of the Deputazione de’ Cinque with the aggiunti. Spada describes the work of the deputation of the Five with its additional members — the body charged with the day-to-day government — and his part in it during the final period of the municipal regime.
The Conclusione is Spada’s summary defence of the whole of his municipal career. He declares that he sacrificed his fortune, suffered the imprisonment of his sons, the tears of his wife and sisters, in the faith of a promised amnesty; that he was constant in upholding the peace treaty; and that in the economic administration no one could convict him of the smallest arbitrariness. He closes with the note that he composed these memoirs exposing even the conduct of the government maintained for some three months under the Austrians, and ends with the words of Bayle on the duty one owes oneself and one’s neighbour to prevent false and exaggerated ideas.
