sources/spada-riflessi-sopra-venezia-par.content:
Riflessi sopra Venezia e voti per la medesima — Parte Terza
Giovanni Andrea Spada, Riflessi sopra Venezia e voti per la medesima (“Reflections on Venice and Wishes for Her”), Brescia, 1801. Part III of the Memorie Apologetiche volume. Essay in Italian. Raw text: 1,378 lines (heavily OCR-garbled 1801 printing).
A companion essay to the autobiographical Part I. Where the memoir defends the author’s own conduct, these Riflessi (“reflections”) step back to trace the long commercial decline of Venice from its height in the fifteenth century to its fall, and close with a set of wishes (voti) for the city’s future under its new masters.
Contents
The essay opens with Venice at the summit of its commercial power — the Republic that enjoyed the privilege of commerce over all Europe and was, by its power, sole mistress of the seas. Spada identifies the two blows that overturned the bases of its wealth: the League of Cambrai, the league of princes raised almost to destroy it, and the contemporary discovery of the Cape of Good Hope, which shifted the world’s trade routes away from the Mediterranean. From then on, he argues, the Republic’s political force declined steadily; whatever energy it later showed in the War of Mantua, the War of Candia or the acquisition of the Morea came from external causes, not any internal spirit of vigour.
He turns to the fifteenth-century commercial system — how Venice, by its position and its political ties, was the centre of all Europe’s commerce at the start of the 1400s, drawing the wealth of Asia through the ports of Syria and Egypt: the drugs, pearls, diamonds and finest cloths; the Spanish wool and Persian silk that fed its workshops; the glass and mirror works; the luxury that, on the testimony of the ambassador to the Diet of Ratisbon, made Venice the object of Europe’s envy. The Senate attracted and commanded all this trade while other sovereigns, distracted by wars of religion and personal rivalry, neglected commerce.
From this summit the essay traces the accumulated causes of decline. Spada describes how, in twenty-five years of open rupture with the Ottoman Porte, the French, English and Dutch inserted themselves into the eastern ports and supplied the silks, wools and glassware that had been almost a Venetian monopoly; how the Venetian Senate drifted into a timid and uncertain policy; how the occupation of the Morea, won through Prince Eugene’s victories and Doge Morosini’s genius, was lost within a few years; and how the Republic’s last naval undertaking, the piratical war, ended in the glory of Cavalier Emo but ruin to Venetian commerce and the Erario.
The essay then examines the decay of the domestic economy — the famous weaving arts of silk and gold, the manufactures of cloth that had supplied the Levant, declining into provincial workshops; the noble landowners of the Terra Ferma turning to agriculture and protecting the rival wool and silk factories of the mainland provinces at the capital’s expense; the maladministration of the customs, the burdensome new duties on the most precious sea-borne goods, the public administration of the Verona customs and the dazi mercanzia that only encouraged smuggling and fed an avaricious ministry.
The final section moves from economic to political collapse. Spada recounts how the radical ills infecting every branch of the public administration had so weakened the state that it entered the war that would invade the Venetian dominion and prepare the fall — without treasury, arsenal, navy or troops, its fortresses half-demolished and the loyalty of the Terra Ferma alienated. During the period of French rule no commercial plan was possible; the maritime force became inert and passed into French hands; the cities beyond the Mincio governed themselves, while even Chioggia imagined becoming a free port for the Cisalpine Republic. He notes how, by the Treaty of Campo Formio, Venice and its provinces up to the Adige passed under the Imperial court, while Istria, Dalmatia and Albania had already met the same fate; and how Venice’s commerce and navigation henceforth depended on powers that were now its rivals — Ferrara, the ports of Romagna, and Trieste above all, which never ceased to emulate her.
The essay closes with the voti (“wishes”) — Spada’s appeal to the Venetians to cooperate in their own happiness, echoing the words he attributes to General Brune telling the Italians to be neither Guelfs nor Ghibellines but brothers, to lay aside their internal divisions, and to rise to liberty and glory, as Genoa had shown them by her example in 1746. He ends with the hope that Venice’s commerce, navy, arts and people may one day compensate France, and with a prayer that the city may be restored to prosperity.
